note: Built by tool/build_mechanics_catalog.py from an open CC0 dataset. Keys: n name, al aliases, c category, g genres, d purpose, s required systems, p parameters with typical range, e edge cases, b common bugs, t balance, a accessibility, r relationships [target, type], k cost profile. Search it with python Claude/hooks/mechanic_catalog.py.

accessibility.adjustable_difficulty.d: A configurable difficulty layer that lets players adjust challenge pressure through explicit modifiers, presets, or assist settings without changing the core content structure.
e: A player changes enemy damage or timing assistance during a boss phase, checkpoint retry, or active multiplayer session.
A fixed-seed challenge or leaderboard run must decide whether modified settings invalidate ranking or use a separate board.
Cloud saves can merge difficulty settings from different devices with different platform defaults.
b: The menu changes setting payloads but active enemies, timers, or encounters keep cached old modifier values.
Assist modifiers affect hidden achievement or leaderboard eligibility without player-facing disclosure.
Per-player local co-op settings overwrite each other because profile ids are stored globally.
t: Each modifier should describe the specific rule it changes so players can choose support without guessing.
Challenge and ranked modes should declare their allowed assist policy before the player invests effort.
a: Make difficulty options available before gameplay starts and from pause menus where technically safe.
Use plain-language descriptions and live previews for timing, damage, hint, and resource changes.

accessibility.assist_mode.d: A named accessibility preset or mode that enables one or more gameplay assists such as timing forgiveness, input help, reduced penalties, or navigation support.
p: assist_feature_ids: timing, aiming, navigation, penalty, input
e: Assist mode is enabled after a checkpoint but before a deterministic challenge result is submitted.
Two local players use different assist modes in the same split-screen or couch co-op session.
A save created with assist features is loaded on a platform where one input helper is unavailable.
b: Assist mode changes UI labels but does not update the feature registry consumed by gameplay systems.
Timing multipliers stack with coyote time and input buffering multiple times after scene reload.
One local player toggles assist mode and changes every player profile in the session.
t: Assist mode should target barriers rather than broadly flattening every system unless the preset clearly says so.
Leaderboard and ranked restrictions should be handled through transparent mode policy, not hidden penalties.
a: Place assist mode near first-launch setup and keep it reachable from pause menus.
Avoid moralized labels; describe practical effects such as wider timing windows or reduced damage.

accessibility.colorblind_modes.d: A set of color and contrast settings that make gameplay, UI, teams, hazards, and feedback readable without relying on color alone.
p: colorblind_filter_id: none, protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, custom
redundant_cue_policy_id: icons, patterns, labels, outlines, combined
preview_scene_id: hud, combat, puzzle, minimap, team_select
e: A color puzzle, team marker, or damage telegraph becomes unsolvable if the mode changes hue but not symbol language.
Post-processing filters can alter screenshots or streaming output differently from actual gameplay materials.
Local multiplayer players may need different color settings on shared or split screens.
b: Only menu UI uses color_palette_id while world-space markers keep hard-coded colors.
Contrast passes in English but fails after localization changes text length and background placement.
Team colors update on the scoreboard but not minimap, outlines, or damage numbers.
t: High-contrast outlines may improve readability for everyone, so competitive games should decide whether they are universal or mode-specific.
Do not use colorblind mode as the only fix for color-dependent puzzles; redundant shapes and labels are more robust.
a: Provide live preview with UI, gameplay markers, minimap, enemy/friendly indicators, and warning states.
Do not communicate critical states by color alone; include symbols, text, position, animation, or pattern differences.

accessibility.text_scaling.d: A readability setting that scales text and related UI layout while preserving interaction targets, localization, safe areas, and overflow behavior.
p: layout_reflow_policy_id: wrap, stack, paginate, scroll, compact
e: Long localized strings at maximum scale need wrapping, scrolling, or pagination without hiding confirm buttons.
Split-screen and handheld modes can require different profile scopes from desktop or living-room displays.
Timed dialogue, tutorials, or captions must remain readable long enough after scaling changes.
b: Text increases but button hit boxes and focus rectangles keep the old dimensions.
Scaled subtitles overlap speaker labels, letterbox bars, or critical HUD warnings.
Layout reflow works in English but clips languages with longer words or different line breaking.
t: Large text should not be treated as a gameplay advantage; design dense HUDs to reflow rather than hide information.
Scaling critical prompts may require reducing noncritical decorative text to preserve screen clarity.
a: Offer live preview and reset controls, and apply changes without requiring restart when possible.
Pair text scaling with contrast, background opacity, and subtitle speaker label settings for real readability.

accessibility.toggle_hold_option.d: A per-action input preference that lets sustained actions use hold, toggle, hybrid, or simplified behavior without changing the action itself.
p: input_action_id: aim, crouch, sprint, block, interact
toggle_reset_context_ids: death, menu, cutscene, weapon_swap, mount
e: Changing the setting while the action is currently active must choose whether to commit, cancel, or convert state.
Toggle aim or crouch should clear on death, respawn, cutscene, mount, and sometimes weapon swap.
Menus and text entry must not accidentally activate gameplay toggles.
b: Changing setting while action is held leaves the action stuck active.
Toggle state is saved as if it were a preference.
Prompt text says hold while behavior is toggle.
t: Accessibility input options should not be treated as difficulty changes unless the action itself changes gameplay timing.
Hybrid modes need careful debounce windows to avoid accidental toggles.
a: Make hold/toggle options available early in settings and near control remapping.
Use prompt text that reflects each player’s current input mode and device.

ai.boss_phase_transition.d: A boss AI state change that swaps goals, attacks, defenses, arena rules, or pacing after defined thresholds or events.
e: Damage crosses multiple thresholds in one hit and the boss must select a deterministic next phase.
A transition starts while the boss is stunned, airborne, grabbed, or in a cinematic animation.
Players die during transition_lock_ms and retry state must restore the correct phase and arena setup.
b: Boss continues an old phase attack after the new phase disables the required hitboxes or arena objects.
Phase transition triggers every frame below the threshold because phase_id is not committed before animation starts.
Checkpoint restores health but not minions, hazards, music state, or attack cooldowns for the current phase.
t: Each phase should teach or remix a readable idea rather than only adding speed and health.
Transition invulnerability can protect spectacle timing but should be communicated clearly to avoid wasted player resources.
a: Use multiple cues for phase changes: animation, UI, audio, subtitles/barks, and arena changes where appropriate.
Avoid full-screen flashes or camera shakes during transitions without reduced-motion and flash-safe settings.

ai.chase.d: An AI pursuit behavior where an agent moves toward a target or last known position until it catches, loses, or abandons the target.
e: The target teleports, climbs, enters a vehicle, or crosses an off-navmesh link the chaser cannot use.
A navmesh_query fails repeatedly and the AI must decide whether to wait, switch route, search, or abandon pursuit.
Target_id ownership changes in multiplayer and chase authority must remain server-side.
b: Path replans every frame and tanks performance when many agents chase the same target.
last_known_position updates through walls because perception_event filtering does not require visibility or valid sound propagation.
Chase animation speed and navigation velocity desynchronize, causing sliding or unfair reach.
t: Short grace windows make stealth resets easy; long windows create pressure but need cover and escape routes.
Pursuit speed should be tuned against player stamina, traversal tools, and level geometry, not in isolation.
a: Show chase state with redundant cues such as music, UI alert markers, enemy barks, or camera-safe indicators.
Avoid chase sequences that require perfect audio localization unless visual route and threat cues are also available.

ai.companion_follow.d: An allied AI behavior where a companion maintains useful proximity to the player while avoiding obstruction, hazards, and unwanted combat mistakes.
e: The player jumps gaps, climbs ladders, enters vehicles, or uses traversal the companion cannot perform.
The companion blocks a doorway, loot pickup, camera view, or precision platforming path.
Combat starts while the companion is catching up or teleporting.
b: Companion replans every frame toward the player's exact position and jitters behind them.
Teleport fallback ignores line of sight or safe placement and appears in front of enemies or hazards.
Companion collision pushes the player off ledges or out of interact prompts.
t: Companions should be useful enough to justify attention but not solve stealth, combat, or traversal for the player by default.
Catch-up rules should be generous in traversal-heavy games and stricter in games where escort positioning is the challenge.
a: Provide commands such as wait, follow, or regroup if companion positioning can interfere with motor or camera control.
Avoid companion chatter or alerts that are audio-only; important ally state should be visible.

ai.cover_seeking.d: An AI positioning behavior where an agent chooses and moves to cover based on threats, sightlines, reservations, and attack options.
e: All nearby cover slots are reserved, unreachable, or exposed to a second target.
Destructible cover disappears while the agent is entering a cover animation.
Tall and low cover require different stance, aim, and hitbox synchronization.
b: Agents choose cover based only on distance and stand on the player's side of the wall.
cover_slot_id reservations never expire after an agent dies or is interrupted.
Cover animation snaps the character out of navmesh position and breaks line-of-sight traces.
t: High-quality cover makes enemies survivable; pair it with flanking routes or destructible counters so fights do not stall.
Too much cover seeking can reduce aggression unless some enemies prefer push, flank, or suppress actions.
a: Use readable silhouettes, barks, or posture changes so players can tell when an enemy is in cover or preparing to peek.
Avoid making tiny exposed limbs the only viable target unless aim assists or alternate tactics exist.

ai.enemy_spawn_director.d: A pacing system that chooses when, where, and what enemies to spawn based on budget, pressure, safety, and encounter goals.
e: All spawn points fail safe placement because they are visible, occupied, unreachable, or behind locked doors.
Spawn budget frees up at the same time multiple directors request enemies.
A player backtracks or speedruns and invalidates the intended encounter region.
b: Director spawns enemies outside navmesh or behind one-way gates because validation only checks distance.
Active enemy count desyncs when enemies die by despawn, fall out of world, or convert allegiance.
Cooldowns reset on save/load and immediately spawn a burst.
t: Spawn budgets should account for enemy role, travel time, player resources, and current objective pressure.
Dynamic spawning needs visible fairness rules; enemies appearing inside cleared safe zones can feel like cheating.
a: Avoid spawning threats directly behind players without readable audio, UI, or camera-safe warning cues.
Offer difficulty settings that change spawn_budget or cooldowns rather than only enemy health.

ai.flee.d: An AI survival behavior where an agent chooses a safer destination away from a threat or hazardous state.
e: All sampled safe destinations are unreachable, closer to another threat, or outside allowed combat bounds.
Several agents choose the same cover or exit and block each other.
The threat disappears during commitment_min_ms, requiring a rule for continue, search, or resume previous state.
b: Agents flee directly away from target_id and run into walls because no navmesh_query evaluates the path.
Threat scores drop below threshold for one frame and cancel flee, creating visible jitter.
Animation root motion continues after AI state changes, moving the agent back toward danger.
t: Frequent flee behavior can make combat feel evasive and slow; reserve it for readable health, morale, or fear states.
Flee destinations should create tactical repositioning, not guaranteed invulnerability or unreachable enemies.
a: Use clear posture, icon, bark, or movement cues so players understand the agent is fleeing rather than bugging out.
Avoid making required targets flee into visually dense spaces without tracking aids or readable silhouettes.

ai.flocking.d: A group movement behavior where agents steer using local cohesion, separation, alignment, and goal forces.
e: Agents pile up at narrow passages where separation fights the goal direction.
A flock splits around an obstacle and needs rules for regrouping or accepting multiple subgroups.
Large swarms exceed performance budgets unless neighbor queries use spatial partitioning.
b: Cohesion and separation weights are both high, causing agents to vibrate in place.
Neighbor queries include dead, hidden, or different flock_id agents and distort steering.
Flocking ignores navmesh or collision constraints and pushes agents through walls.
t: Swarm density affects difficulty as much as individual enemy stats; too much separation may make a swarm harmless.
Readable group motion is usually better than perfect physical realism for combat and navigation.
a: Avoid dense, fast, high-contrast swarms that obscure hazards or overwhelm visual processing without options.
Provide target highlighting or reduced visual clutter when flocking agents are required targets.

ai.investigate_noise.d: An AI behavior where an agent reacts to an auditory or disturbance event by moving to inspect its source or last known position.
e: Several noise events arrive in one decision interval and need deterministic priority ordering.
A noise source is unreachable, inside a wall, or outside the agent's allowed zone.
The agent hears a noise while already chasing a target and must compare threat_score against curiosity.
b: Investigation uses the sound emitter transform after it has moved instead of the captured event position.
AI forgets the original patrol_route_id and cannot resume after investigation_duration_ms.
Every nearby agent responds identically because squad_id coordination or reservation is missing.
t: Noise tools should be reliable enough for planning but limited by line, distance, cooldown, or enemy suspicion state.
If investigation always escalates to chase, players stop using distractions as stealth tools.
a: Show or teach which player actions make noise, using visual indicators as well as sound.
For players with hearing loss, provide readable suspicion markers or minimap pulses for caused distractions.

ai.line_of_sight_detection.d: A perception test that decides whether an AI can currently see a target through field of view, distance, occlusion, and visibility rules.
e: The target is partly visible behind cover and only some occlusion probes pass.
Transparent, one-way, destructible, or foliage materials need explicit visibility rules.
Fast-moving targets cross the cone between decision ticks and may need interpolation or grace.
b: Raycasts start inside the AI collider or target collider and report false occlusion.
Sight checks run in render update while AI decisions run in fixed ticks, creating inconsistent detection.
FOV math ignores vertical angle and detects targets above or below through floors.
t: Wide cones and long ranges need strong cover tools or stealth becomes impossible.
Grace windows make detection feel less flickery but can make quick peeks unexpectedly dangerous.
a: Represent detection state with readable UI or enemy posture changes, not only subtle audio stingers.
Avoid color-only visibility feedback; combine meters, icons, text labels, or contrast-safe highlights.

ai.patrol.d: An AI navigation behavior where an agent follows a defined route, schedule, or area loop while monitoring perception events.
e: A navmesh_query to the next waypoint fails because a door closed, a moving platform left, or dynamic blockers appeared.
After chase or investigation, the agent must decide whether to resume from nearest waypoint, saved waypoint_index, or a designer-authored fallback.
Multiple agents sharing patrol_route_id need offset timing or avoidance so they do not stack on the same waypoint.
b: waypoint_index advances even when movement failed, causing the patrol to skip coverage-critical points.
Patrol resumes immediately after losing the player because investigation state clears before line-of-sight grace expires.
Look arcs snap at waypoints and unfairly detect the player during an animation/state synchronization pop.
t: Long predictable routes reward planning; randomized routes need visible tells or they become perceived as unfair.
Coverage should intentionally leave timing windows, alternate tools, or route manipulation options for the player.
a: Expose facing, suspicion, and route timing through readable visual cues as well as audio.
Avoid requiring players to memorize long invisible schedules without landmarks, map hints, or repeated route tells.

ai.utility_scoring.d: A decision model where candidate actions are scored from current context and the AI commits to the best suitable option.
e: All candidate actions score zero or fail validation and the AI needs a safe fallback action.
Two actions repeatedly tie and must resolve by deterministic decision order rather than random flicker.
A high-scoring action becomes invalid between scoring and commit, such as cover being reserved or target_id dying.
b: Score curves are normalized inconsistently, so one blackboard_key dominates every decision.
AI switches actions every decision_interval_ms because hysteresis_margin or commitment_min_ms is missing.
Debug output shows final score but not contribution breakdown, making tuning impossible.
t: Score curves should be tuned from observed encounters; theoretical priority values often fail once actions combine.
Commitment windows make AI readable but too much commitment can make agents ignore urgent threats.
a: Readable intent cues such as windups, barks, or posture changes help players understand why AI suddenly changes tactics.
Avoid perfect reaction scoring for required counterplay; give players timing windows after AI commits to an action.

camera.camera_lock_on.d: A camera mode that frames a selected target while preserving enough control for movement and combat.
e: Large bosses may need multiple lock anchors rather than a single root transform.
Targets dying, teleporting, becoming invisible, or entering cutscenes should clear or retarget predictably.
Line-of-sight grace must handle pillars and brief occlusion without keeping lock through entire walls.
b: Camera locks to a target pivot inside the mesh and clips into large enemies.
Stick drift repeatedly cycles targets because target switching lacks deadzone and cooldown.
Lock-on rotates the character but not attack traces, causing attacks to miss the locked target.
t: Strong lock-on improves readability in duels but can reduce threat from flanking enemies.
Target switching should be predictable enough for crowded fights without automatically selecting the safest option.
a: Provide clear target indicators, reticle size options, and camera sensitivity controls for lock-on mode.
Offer reduced camera auto-rotation or slower orbit speeds for players sensitive to rapid camera movement.

camera.camera_zoom.d: A camera behavior that changes field of view or orthographic scale to show more detail or more surrounding space.
e: Zooming into walls or ceilings should shorten distance without pushing the camera through collision.
UI scale and reticle placement must remain readable at both minimum and maximum zoom.
Cutscenes, lock-on, photo mode, and dialogue can all request zoom; priority and restore rules must be explicit.
b: Zoom target is applied to FOV and camera distance at the same time, doubling the perceived effect.
Camera collision runs before zoom interpolation and causes popping in tight spaces.
Manual zoom is lost after respawn because default camera state overwrites player preference.
t: Wide zoom improves awareness but can reduce tension, surprise, or precision reading of nearby hazards.
Aim or inspection zoom should usually trade awareness, movement, or input commitment for the extra detail it grants.
a: Provide zoom speed controls or instant-step options for players sensitive to animated camera scaling.
Avoid using zoom alone as critical feedback; pair it with stable UI, sound, or object highlighting.

camera.cinematic_camera.d: A directed camera mode that uses authored shots, cuts, blends, and control locks to frame scripted or dramatic moments.
p: shot_timeline_id: timeline asset or sequence id
e: A cinematic starts while the player is in lock-on, split screen, photo mode, or a multiplayer spectator camera.
Skipping the shot must restore camera mode, input locks, subtitles, and pending gameplay triggers exactly once.
Save/load during a cinematic needs either a safe replay point or restored gameplay camera state.
b: Camera priority remains on the cinematic shot after the sequence ends or is skipped.
A cut triggers twice and fires the same gameplay event or subtitle cue twice.
Player control unlocks before the camera restores collision and occlusion handling.
t: Cinematic shots should be brief or skippable when repeated after failure.
Camera control locks are acceptable for story emphasis but risky during active gameplay hazards.
a: Respect reduced-motion settings for handheld sway, rapid cuts, field-of-view shifts, and shake layered into the shot.
Keep subtitles and speaker labels synchronized with cinematic timing, including skip and pause behavior.

camera.dynamic_fov.d: A field-of-view adjustment that responds to speed, sprinting, boosting, aiming, or other gameplay states.
e: ADS, scopes, cutscenes, vehicles, and sprint can request conflicting FOV profiles; priority must be deterministic.
High FOV on ultrawide displays can distort reticles and weapon models if presentation is not separated.
Rapidly entering and leaving sprint can create pulsing unless blends are debounced.
b: FOV offset is added repeatedly every frame instead of blended from a base value.
Reduced-motion settings scale camera shake but not dynamic FOV.
Weapon viewmodel FOV and world camera FOV desynchronize during sprint transitions.
t: Dynamic FOV can make movement feel faster than it is; tune speed perception alongside actual movement values.
Large FOV shifts should be reserved for strong state changes such as boost, not every small velocity fluctuation.
a: Expose a dynamic-FOV intensity slider and allow disabling the effect without changing gameplay speed.
Avoid stacking dynamic FOV with screen shake and camera roll unless reduced-motion settings scale all of them together.

camera.first_person_camera.d: A camera viewpoint placed at or near the avatar's eyes to make the player see from the character's perspective.
e: Crouch, prone, swimming, ladders, vehicles, and cutscenes all need explicit eye-height transition rules.
Camera placement near walls should avoid seeing through geometry without pushing the player body backward.
Viewmodel weapon motion should not change projectile origin unless the design intentionally models muzzle position.
b: The camera inherits animation head jitter and causes nausea or aiming instability.
Near clipping lets the player see through doors or walls by standing close to them.
Projectile traces originate from the weapon model while the reticle uses camera center, causing visible misses.
t: First-person viewpoints increase precision and tension but reduce peripheral awareness compared with third-person cameras.
Headbob, weapon sway, and recoil should support feel without obscuring required information.
a: Expose FOV, headbob, weapon sway, camera shake, and sensitivity settings independently.
Provide reticle and subtitle options because first-person presentation often uses small center-screen cues.

camera.screen_shake.d: A short camera offset, rotation, or impulse profile used to emphasize impact while preserving play readability.
e: Repeated rapid events should accumulate through a cap rather than stacking into unreadable camera motion.
Reticles, health bars, subtitles, and interaction prompts should not inherit shake unless the UI is intentionally diegetic.
Pausing during a shake should define whether decay freezes, completes instantly, or resumes from remaining trauma.
b: Shake is applied before camera collision and pushes the camera through walls.
Multiple systems write offsets independently and fight or double the final displacement.
Reduced-motion settings scale visual shake but not vibration, audio rumble, or FOV pulses.
t: Use small shake profiles frequently and reserve large profiles for events that deserve momentary attention.
Camera motion should never be required to understand damage direction, hit confirmation, or timing.
a: Expose intensity and disable options, and pair impacts with non-motion cues such as hit flash, sound, haptics, or UI markers.
Avoid high-frequency or sustained shake patterns that can cause discomfort or obscure precision tasks.

camera.smooth_follow_camera.d: A camera behavior that follows a target with damping, lookahead, dead zones, or catch-up rules instead of hard snapping.
e: Respawn, fast travel, teleport blink, or room transitions should snap or blend from a known state.
Camera bounds can conflict with lookahead near level edges and reveal empty space or hide hazards.
Moving platforms and elevators need vertical follow tuning that avoids seasick lag.
b: Damping uses frame-based interpolation and feels different at 30 FPS and 144 FPS.
Lookahead changes direction instantly on input reversal and causes camera wobble.
Camera remains outside level bounds after a teleport because bounds are applied before snapping.
t: More smoothing feels cinematic but can hide sudden hazards in fast platformers.
Lookahead should support intended movement direction without showing offscreen secrets too early.
a: Expose camera smoothing and lookahead intensity options when camera lag can affect comfort or precision.
Avoid oscillating follow behavior; stable camera motion helps players with motion sensitivity and spatial tracking needs.

camera.split_screen.d: A local multiplayer camera layout that assigns each player a viewport, camera owner, safe-area rules, and UI scaling profile.
e: A player joins or leaves while another player is in a menu, cutscene, vehicle, or lock-on camera.
One viewport needs subtitles, prompts, or accessibility settings that differ from another local player.
Four-player layouts can make minimaps, text, and target indicators unreadable without UI scaling changes.
b: Input focus goes to the wrong player after layout changes.
UI uses full-screen coordinates instead of viewport_rect and appears in another player’s view.
Camera effects such as shake, FOV, or post-process settings bleed between players.
t: Small viewports reduce peripheral vision, so enemies, prompts, and hazards may need closer telegraphs.
Dynamic split/merge can improve screen space but may be disorienting without stable rules.
a: Allow per-player UI scale, subtitle visibility, camera shake, and color settings where possible.
Avoid tiny text and low-contrast markers in split layouts; test from couch distance.

camera.third_person_camera.d: A camera viewpoint that follows behind, above, or beside the player avatar while keeping the character visible.
e: Tight corridors should shorten camera distance without hiding the avatar or rapidly popping.
Aiming, lock-on, climbing, swimming, and vehicles can all request different third-person profiles.
Camera collision should ignore small foliage but respect walls, ceilings, and large moving objects.
b: Camera snaps when occlusion clears because the desired distance is restored instantly.
Avatar blocks the reticle or interact prompt at common shoulder offsets.
Recenter fights player input because manual-control cooldown is too short.
t: Closer cameras increase tension and character presence; farther cameras improve awareness and traversal planning.
Combat cameras should preserve threat visibility without automatically solving positioning for the player.
a: Expose orbit sensitivity, inversion, recenter strength, shoulder side, and camera distance where possible.
Offer reduced camera acceleration and motion options for players sensitive to rapid orbiting.

camera.top_down_camera.d: A camera mode that views the play space from above or at an angled overhead perspective while tracking targets within screen-space bounds.
e: Tall walls, roofs, trees, and bridges can hide the player or target unless occlusion policy is explicit.
Mouse/cursor aiming and gamepad aiming may need different camera_target_id or cursor weighting rules.
Zooming out can reveal spoiler areas, hidden rooms, or enemies behind fog-of-war bounds.
b: Camera follows raw player position and jitters when the character collides with dense geometry.
Input-relative movement changes when the camera yaw or map rotation changes without remapping controls.
Occlusion fades the wrong roof or leaves invisible collision blocking the view.
t: Wider zoom improves planning but can reduce surprise and reveal encounter setup.
Strict screen-space bounds make the camera stable; loose bounds make fast movement feel more responsive.
a: Provide zoom options, high-contrast outlines, and reduced camera smoothing for players who need clearer spatial tracking.
Avoid critical information hidden only by vertical depth cues; use shadows, labels, or outlines.

combat.aim_down_sights.d: A focused aiming state that narrows view or reticle behavior to improve precision.
e: Entering ADS while sprinting, reloading, climbing, or swimming needs priority rules.
High zoom can break camera collision or reticle placement near walls.
Toggle ADS should clear on weapon swap, death, and menus.
b: Sensitivity changes stack every time ADS is entered.
Projectile origin remains hip-fire while reticle uses scoped camera.
FOV changes do not respect user motion settings.
t: ADS should improve precision enough to matter while costing awareness, mobility, or readiness.
Strong aim assist in ADS can overwhelm manual skill if target switching is too sticky.
a: Offer hold/toggle settings, scoped sensitivity, reticle options, and reduced zoom-motion settings.

combat.area_of_effect_attack.d: An attack that affects multiple targets or positions inside a defined radius, shape, cone, line, or zone.
p: aoe_shape: circle, sphere, cone, box, line
e: Targets partly inside the area need center-point, collider-overlap, or coverage rules.
Line of sight and cover should decide whether walls block the effect.
Multiple overlapping areas can stack, refresh, or choose the strongest effect.
b: Visual radius and damage radius use different scale values.
The area hits targets every frame instead of once per attack instance.
Falloff applies twice because both attack and damage systems reduce the value.
t: Large radius, short telegraph, and high damage together leave little counterplay.
Persistent zones should be balanced through duration, visibility, stacking, and escape options.
a: Use clear telegraph shapes, high-contrast edges, and non-color cues before damage occurs.
Avoid effects that hide their own safe zones with particles or screen shake.

combat.block.d: A defensive state that reduces, redirects, or prevents eligible incoming damage within defined limits.
e: Area attacks and explosions need rules for whether guard angle or distance matters more.
Blocking while airborne, crouched, stunned, climbing, or reloading should have explicit priority.
Guard break at zero stamina must clear block state before applying follow-up hit reactions.
b: Block checks use the attacker's facing instead of the defender's guard arc.
Stamina reaches zero after damage reduction, allowing one extra free block.
Hold block remains active after weapon swap or animation cancel.
t: High reduction and low stamina cost make block dominant; chip damage and guard break preserve pressure.
Enemies need visible answers to block, but unblockable attacks should be signaled before commitment.
a: Support hold and toggle guard if blocking is sustained for long encounters.
Use distinct indicators for blockable, guard-breaking, and unblockable attacks where readability is critical.

combat.charged_attack.d: An attack that grows, changes, or unlocks after the player holds input for a defined charge window.
e: Damage, stun, dodge, weapon swap, or resource loss during charge must define cancel and refund behavior.
Charge state during pause, slow motion, or hit stop should use one clock.
Input release on the same frame as full charge needs deterministic level selection.
b: Charge continues after the button is released because input-up events are missed during UI focus changes.
Charge damage stacks every frame after full charge and exceeds intended multiplier.
Animation shows full charge but combat metadata still uses undercharged values.
t: Higher charge payoff should come with exposure, resource cost, clear telegraphing, or reduced mobility.
Partial-charge usefulness prevents the mechanic from feeling binary and wasted when interrupted.
a: Offer hold/toggle or charge-confirm alternatives where long button holds are common.
Use audio, visual, and haptic cues for charge levels rather than relying on small particles alone.

combat.combo_chain.d: A sequence system where attacks can link into later actions through timing, hit state, input windows, or cancel rules.
e: Inputs during hit stop, pause, slow motion, or rollback need one authoritative buffer clock.
Whiffed attacks should define whether they can chain, only recover, or cancel into defense.
Changing weapons or targets mid-chain must clear or translate the current combo index.
b: Queued input triggers twice because both animation event and state update consume it.
Combo index fails to reset after interruption and the next attack starts at step three.
Attack cancel metadata differs between client and server, causing desync in networked combat.
t: Long chains need escape valves such as pushback, resource limits, decay, or defensive cancels.
High-damage finishers should require commitment, positioning, or hit confirmation.
a: Support input buffering and readable cancel windows rather than requiring exact frame-perfect presses for basic chains.
Use training or tutorial prompts to expose combo routes without relying on hidden notation.

combat.critical_hit.d: A high-impact hit result caused by chance, precision, vulnerability, or build rules.
e: Damage over time, area attacks, summons, and reflected projectiles need eligibility rules.
Critical chance above 100% can convert to extra damage, multi-crit tiers, or be clamped.
Guaranteed crit buffs must define whether they are consumed on blocked, immune, or missed attacks.
b: Critical multiplier applies before and after armor reduction unintentionally.
Weak-point hits also roll random critical and double dip without design approval.
UI shows critical feedback for zero-damage immune hits.
t: Random crits add excitement but can undermine fairness in competitive or precision-heavy games.
Deterministic weak-point crits reward mastery and can be balanced through aiming difficulty and exposure windows.
a: Use shape, text, sound, or hit-marker variation in addition to color for critical feedback.
Avoid making tiny weak points mandatory without aim assists, alternate strategies, or readable target presentation.

combat.damage_over_time.d: A status effect that applies damage across multiple ticks after application.
e: Applying the same DoT from multiple sources needs ownership and stacking rules.
Damage ticks during pause, invulnerability, or death state should be explicit.
Cleansing at the same moment as a tick needs deterministic ordering.
b: Tick timers drift and deal extra damage over long fights.
Refreshing duration also doubles stack count unintentionally.
Kill credit is lost because the source entity despawned before the final tick.
t: High total damage needs counterplay through cleanse, resistance, or avoidance.
Short tick intervals feel responsive but can create UI noise and performance load.
a: Use icons, timers, color-safe overlays, and audio cues to show active harmful statuses.

combat.guard_break.d: An attack or pressure state that defeats blocking and leaves the defender vulnerable.
e: Guard break and health damage landing on the same frame need deterministic ordering.
Bosses may need partial stagger rather than full vulnerability.
Multiple attackers can stack pressure too quickly without caps.
b: Guard meter goes negative and never recovers.
Break stun can be canceled by holding block again.
UI guard meter updates after the break and appears unfair.
t: Guard break should punish passive defense without making block useless.
Recovery windows should account for enemy combo length and multiplayer focus fire.
a: Use strong audio/visual warnings as guard nears break, not only a small meter.

combat.hit_stun.d: A temporary state after being hit where an actor loses or limits control before recovering.
e: Hit stun during jumps, ladders, grapples, cutscenes, or dialogue needs priority and recovery rules.
Multiple rapid hits should stack, refresh, or decay rather than locking actors forever.
Hit stop and hit stun should use separate clocks so visual freeze does not extend gameplay stun unexpectedly.
b: Input lockout remains after stun animation is interrupted.
Hit stop pauses projectiles but not timers, causing mismatched follow-up windows.
Stun applies twice because damage event and animation event both trigger reaction.
t: Long hit stun enables combos but can remove agency or create infinite loops without decay.
Short hit stun preserves control but may make attacks feel weightless unless paired with hit stop or animation reaction.
a: Use clear recovery cues so players know when control returns.
Avoid rapid repeated stun flashes that obscure hazards or cause visual discomfort.

combat.invincibility_frames.d: A temporary damage-immunity window that lets an actor ignore eligible hits from specific sources while preserving state priority and readable feedback.
e: A lingering area hit overlaps the exact first or last immunity tick and needs inclusive boundary rules.
Two immunity sources overlap with different bypass damage type rules.
A networked client predicts i-frames but the server receives the damage event on a different tick.
b: Invulnerability is driven only by animation events and changes when animation playback changes.
Damage resolver checks immunity after applying hit stun, knockback, or damage numbers.
Overlapping immunity sources clear each other in the wrong order and leave the actor permanently immune or exposed.
t: Long immunity windows lower execution pressure but can turn evasive actions into universal defense.
Bypass damage types should be rare and well-telegraphed, or players will stop trusting i-frames.
a: Use readable attack telegraphs and optional assist settings for games that rely on narrow immunity timing.
Pair immunity feedback with visual and audio cues, but avoid intense flashing for players with sensitivity settings.

combat.knockback.d: A hit reaction that displaces an actor away from an impact, explosion, source direction, or authored vector.
e: Knockback into walls, pits, slopes, water, or moving platforms needs stable collision behavior.
Multiple hits in one frame should stack, take the strongest, or refresh according to rules.
Invulnerable, armored, blocking, or stunned targets need knockback eligibility metadata.
b: Transform movement bypasses collision and pushes targets through walls.
Knockback direction uses attacker facing instead of actual impact normal.
Control lockout is never cleared after landing or wall collision.
t: High knockback can be stronger than damage when hazards, ledges, or crowd control matter.
Resistance and armor let large enemies feel stable without removing feedback entirely.
a: Use clear pre-hit telegraphs for attacks that cause large displacement or ring-outs.
Avoid excessive camera motion during knockback, or provide reduced impact-camera settings.

combat.lock_on_targeting.d: A targeting mode that keeps combat focus, camera framing, or attacks oriented toward a selected target.
e: Target death, despawn, stealth, or phase transition must choose the next target or clear lock cleanly.
Large bosses with multiple weak points need target anchors that do not pull camera into geometry.
Crowds can cause target cycling to skip expected enemies if screen-space and distance scores disagree.
b: The camera locks to the target root instead of a visible anchor and clips through the floor or body.
Target switching fires from stick drift because no deadzone or cooldown is applied.
Line-of-sight traces hit the player's own weapon or shield and break lock incorrectly.
t: Strong lock-on increases combat readability but can reduce spatial awareness in group fights.
Target assist should help intended attacks connect without invalidating manual aim or positioning.
a: Offer lock-on reticle size/color options and clear target-switch controls.
Provide camera sensitivity and auto-recenter settings to reduce motion discomfort during lock-on.

combat.melee_attack.d: A close-range attack that uses a hitbox, weapon arc, overlap volume, or trace near the attacker.
e: Fast movement during active frames should not let the hitbox skip through small targets.
One swing must define whether it can hit one target once, many targets once, or the same target repeatedly.
Attacking near walls should handle weapon clipping and blocked arcs consistently.
b: Damage is applied every frame of overlap because hit targets are not tracked per attack instance.
Hitboxes spawn from animated bones that update after physics, causing one-frame visual mismatch.
Attack range differs between left and right facing due to unmirrored offsets.
t: Long reach and low recovery make melee safe; slower recovery or commitment preserves enemy counterplay.
Hit stun, knockback, and cancel windows should be balanced together because they determine whether pressure loops are possible.
a: Use clear hit confirmation through impact sound, hit flash, controller vibration, or hit markers.
Avoid requiring hidden animation-frame knowledge for basic attacks; reserve tight cancels for advanced mastery.

combat.parry.d: A precisely timed defensive action that turns an incoming attack into advantage.
e: Multi-hit attacks must specify whether one parry covers all hits or only the first strike.
Projectile ownership should transfer or be destroyed without damaging the parrying player later.
Parry during rollback, pause, hit stop, or slow motion must use one timing clock.
b: The active window is tied to animation frames and changes when animation playback rate changes.
Both parry success and damage are applied because hit resolution order is inconsistent.
Parry effects trigger on friendly or environmental hits that should be ignored.
t: A generous active window can make parry replace block and dodge unless failure recovery or eligibility limits matter.
Rewards should match risk: safe parries need modest payoff, while strict parries can justify large stagger or counter windows.
a: Pair parryable attacks with readable windups, audio cues, or optional indicators.
Offer timing-window assists or alternate defensive options if parry is required for progression.

combat.projectile_reflection.d: A defensive or reactive action that redirects an incoming projectile back, away, or toward a new target.
e: Explosive, homing, beam, hitscan, and area projectiles need explicit reflect eligibility.
Ownership transfer must prevent reflected shots from damaging the reflector's allies unless intended.
Reflecting a projectile on the same frame it expires or hits another target needs ordering rules.
b: Projectile changes direction visually but damage owner remains the original attacker.
Reflected projectile immediately collides with the reflector because it spawns inside their collider.
Homing projectiles keep tracking the player after reflection.
t: Wide reflection windows can invalidate ranged enemies unless limited by stamina, cooldown, angle, or projectile tags.
Reflect damage multipliers should be tuned against enemy health and projectile frequency.
a: Use readable projectile silhouettes and reflect cues when timing is required.
Offer alternate defenses if reflection is mandatory and depends on very narrow timing.

combat.ranged_attack.d: An attack that applies damage or effects from a distance through projectiles, traces, beams, or targeting rules.
p: projectile_spawn_offset: weapon muzzle or actor center
e: Firing near cover should not spawn projectiles behind walls or inside the shooter's collision.
Very fast projectiles need continuous collision or sub-stepping to avoid tunneling.
Projectile ownership must handle reflection, friendly fire, despawn, and save/load boundaries.
b: Projectile visuals and damage traces use different origins, causing visible misses to hit.
Ammo is consumed before server rejection and not refunded after prediction correction.
Spread uses frame-random state and breaks deterministic replays or seeded runs.
t: Long reach needs counter-pressure such as reload, ammo, spread, travel, cover, recoil, or enemy mobility.
Projectile travel gives defenders readable counterplay; hitscan needs stronger aim or exposure constraints.
a: Offer reticle scaling, color options, aim assist settings, and clear impact feedback where precision aiming is central.
Use hit markers or impact effects so players can distinguish misses, armor hits, blocked shots, and immune targets.

combat.reload.d: A committed action that transfers ammunition into a weapon before it can fire again.
e: Reload interrupted by sprint, damage, weapon swap, or cutscene needs ammo transfer rules.
Save/load, reconnect, or rollback during reload must restore reload_started_at_ms, commit state, magazine count, reserve count, and cancel policy together.
Per-shell or staged reloads need rules for partial completion when reserve ammo runs out mid-sequence.
b: Ammo is added at animation start and duplicated after cancel.
Reload finishes visually but weapon state remains unable to fire.
Inventory reserve can go negative after rapid weapon switching.
t: Long reload windows create tactical exposure; short reloads make ammo mostly cosmetic.
Per-round reloads are more flexible and should cost less total vulnerability per partial refill.
a: Use clear magazine and reserve indicators and avoid relying only on click sounds for empty weapons.

combat.shield.d: A defensive layer or equipment mechanic that absorbs, blocks, regenerates, or redirects incoming damage.
e: Damage overflow after shield break must decide whether excess damage carries to health.
Damage over time, poison, environmental hazards, and falls need explicit shield interaction.
Shield recharge should pause, reset, or continue during cutscenes, menus, and respawn according to design.
b: Shield absorbs unblockable or environmental damage because damage type filters are ignored.
Recharge starts every frame after a hit and never respects the delay.
Overflow damage is applied twice when shield breaks.
t: Regenerating shields encourage cover and disengagement; finite shields encourage resource conservation.
Shield counters should be readable enough that players understand why protection failed.
a: Use clear shield capacity and break feedback through sound, UI, and visual state, not only subtle shader changes.
Avoid high-frequency shield flicker effects without intensity controls.

combat.stealth_kill.d: A high-reward attack performed from concealment, surprise, or a vulnerable target state.
e: The target turning during prompt display should either preserve eligibility briefly or cancel before input.
Nearby witnesses need line-of-sight and hearing checks before alarm state changes.
Large enemies, bosses, vehicles, and scripted NPCs need explicit immune or special-case metadata.
b: Prompt appears through walls because eligibility uses distance but not visibility.
The target dies before animation alignment completes, leaving the player locked in place.
Body discovery logic runs before the takedown finishes and alerts the room instantly.
t: Instant takedowns should be gated by awareness, enemy type, animation commitment, or post-kill consequences.
Noise and body management keep stealth kills from removing all encounter pressure.
a: Use a clear prompt with configurable size and avoid color-only eligibility changes.
Allow prompt hold or confirm settings so accidental takedowns do not punish motor control differences.

crafting.crafting_queue.d: Crafting jobs are placed into ordered slots and complete after station, recipe, and progress rules are satisfied.
p: craft_started_at_ms: server timestamp or simulation tick
e: A station is destroyed, moved, or loses fuel while it has active and pending queue slots.
The player cancels a job on the same tick that completion is being claimed.
Offline progress completes several jobs while the output inventory is full.
b: Completed jobs grant output every login because completion_claimed is not persisted.
Cancellation refunds ingredients after the output has already been produced by the server.
Queue sorting changes queue_slot_index without updating UI selection, causing cancellation of the wrong job.
t: Queue length controls production scale; too many slots can remove meaningful station and storage decisions.
Long jobs work best when players can plan, cancel, or reprioritize without losing opaque amounts of progress.
a: Show job order, remaining progress, cancellation outcome, and blocked output state in readable text.
Support keyboard and controller queue reordering without requiring precise drag gestures.

crafting.ingredient_quality.d: Ingredients carry grade metadata that can affect recipe eligibility, output stats, yield, failure, or rarity.
p: ingredient_quality_tier: crude, common, fine, superior, pristine
e: A stack contains mixed item_instance_id quality tiers but the UI treats it as one uniform ingredient.
Preview uses the highest possible output while server validation uses the actual selected ingredients.
A recipe accepts substitutions but the output name, stats, or icon still assume the default material.
b: Ingredient quality is stored only on item definitions, so every instance of the material has the same grade.
Random output rolls are not seeded by transaction_id and produce different results on client and server.
The crafting UI auto-selects rare ingredients for low-value recipes without warning the player.
t: Quality tiers are most useful when they change meaningful stats or yields, not only item color.
Low-tier materials should remain useful through bulk recipes, repairs, or substitutions so gathering stays rewarding.
a: Represent quality with text labels and icons, not color alone.
Warn clearly before consuming high-grade ingredients in recipes where grade has little or no effect.

crafting.recipe_crafting.d: A player converts specific ingredients into defined outputs by executing a validated recipe transaction.
e: The player confirms a recipe while another transaction removes one required ingredient from the inventory.
The recipe is migrated between content versions and old save data references an obsolete recipe_id.
The output stack cannot fit after ingredients have already been reserved for consumption.
b: Ingredients are consumed but the output is not granted because capacity validation runs after deletion.
Rapid double-clicks submit two transaction_id values and produce duplicate outputs from one ingredient set.
Recipe previews use display-only substitution rules that do not match server validation.
t: Recipe costs should create meaningful gathering goals without forcing players into repetitive low-value collection.
Recipes that unlock core survival tools should be discoverable early and not depend on rare random drops.
a: Show missing ingredients, station requirements, and inventory capacity failures in text as well as icons.
Allow confirmation flows that do not require repeated rapid clicks for large batches.

crafting.workbench.d: A placed or discovered station grants access to recipes, queues, upgrades, or crafting rules tied to its tier and location.
e: The player moves out of interaction_radius_units while a confirmation dialog or queue edit is open.
A station is upgraded, destroyed, or claimed by another player while a craft is pending.
Recipes are visible because of player unlocks but blocked by station tier, missing tool, or fuel requirements.
b: UI caches a recipe list from the previous station and allows invalid crafting at a lower-tier workbench.
Queue outputs are claimable by players without access_permission_id rights.
Station upgrades change tier but do not migrate existing queue entries or recipe filters.
t: Station tiers should unlock distinct capabilities, not only small percentage improvements.
Portable stations reduce friction but can weaken exploration, base defense, and settlement progression.
a: Show station tier, blocked requirements, and access permissions in text within the crafting UI.
Keep station interaction prompts stable and remappable for players using controller or assistive input.

economy.coins.d: A spendable currency balance used as the default unit for rewards, purchases, fees, and sinks.
e: A reward grant would exceed wallet_capacity and needs a cap, overflow bank, or explicit rejection message.
A purchase and reward arrive in the same frame or server tick and must resolve in a deterministic transaction order.
Refunds after a failed purchase must restore the exact debit amount and currency_id, not a recalculated current price.
b: Wallet UI increments optimistically but the server rejects the transaction, leaving the client balance wrong until reload.
Coin rewards use floats for display and storage, creating rounding drift after many small grants.
Sellback, repair, and upgrade systems each use different currency IDs for what players see as the same coin balance.
t: Track source and sink totals by currency_source_id and currency_sink_id; inflation is easier to fix when the dominant faucet is visible.
Early prices should teach the value of coins, while late sinks need enough capacity to absorb farming without making casual play feel stalled.
a: Show wallet changes as readable deltas with icons and text, not only tiny animated numbers.
Use grouping separators or compact notation options for large balances so players can distinguish 10000 from 100000 quickly.

economy.crafting_materials.d: Collectible resources consumed by recipes, upgrades, repairs, or conversions instead of acting as direct currency.
e: A recipe consumes several material_id values and one stack changes between preview and commit.
A material is removed from a live build but still exists in old saves, loot tables, or recipes.
Inventory is full when a drop grants a required material, so the game needs overflow, conversion, or protected pickup rules.
b: Crafting preview subtracts materials locally and the committed transaction subtracts them again.
Recipe validation checks display names instead of material_id, breaking when localization changes.
Stack split and merge operations lose item_instance_id metadata for enhanced or bound materials.
t: Pair each important material with at least one reliable source and one desirable sink so farming feels intentional.
Rare materials should not be required in large quantities for basic progression unless there is pity, conversion, or targeted acquisition.
a: Show material names, icons, and source hints together so players are not forced to memorize small icons.
Provide recipe pinning or tracking for players who need persistent reminders of required material counts.

economy.dynamic_pricing.d: A pricing rule set that changes item costs or sell values based on context, demand, reputation, scarcity, or time.
e: A price changes between confirmation and commit, so the transaction must decide whether to honor the quoted price or reject it.
Discounts and sellback ratios can combine into a profitable buy-sell loop if final prices are not checked together.
Vendor stock refreshes while the player has a purchase dialog open.
b: UI displays rounded prices while the transaction debits unrounded minor units, creating visible balance mismatches.
Client-side discount calculations are trusted by the server and allow edited price requests.
Price caches do not invalidate after reputation or stock changes, so players see stale prices.
t: Keep the visible reason for a price change close to the price display so players can plan rather than guess.
Simulate repeated buying and selling with all modifiers active; arbitrage bugs often appear only after several systems combine.
a: Show final price, previous price, and reason for change in text as well as color.
Avoid time-limited price changes that require rushed decisions unless the player can review the item details comfortably.

economy.gacha_pull.d: A paid or earned random reward draw from a published pool, often with rarity tiers and duplicate handling.
e: Currency is debited but reward grant fails because inventory is full or the item definition is missing.
A banner expires between preview and commit, so the server must reject or honor the request consistently.
A duplicate reward triggers conversion and pity progress in the same pull.
b: Pity counters increment on preview or failed pulls instead of committed reward grants.
Client-side RNG selects the reward and can be manipulated or desynced from server logs.
Published odds differ from configured rarity_tier_weights after banner filters are applied.
t: Simulate expected pulls to featured rewards, worst-case pity outcomes, and duplicate conversion value before pricing the banner.
If real money can influence pulls, transparency and regional compliance matter as much as reward tuning.
a: Show odds, pity progress, duplicate conversion results, and spending confirmation in readable text.
Allow long animations to be skipped or reduced, especially for repeated multi-pulls.

economy.idle_income.d: A recurring resource grant that accrues while the player waits, plays, upgrades generators, or returns after time away.
e: The player changes device time or resumes from sleep with a negative or enormous elapsed interval.
A generator is upgraded, sold, or disabled while unclaimed income exists.
Offline income reaches cap before the player returns, so further time should not inflate the wallet.
b: Income uses frame delta while the app is backgrounded and grants a burst after resume without cap checks.
Upgrading a generator retroactively applies the new income_rate_per_minute to all previous offline time.
Claim UI shows projected income but the committed transaction uses a different elapsed time source.
t: Idle income should support, not replace, active play unless the whole game is built around idle progression.
Offline caps and generator upgrade costs control return-session pacing more than the raw rate alone.
a: Let players claim income through clear buttons and summaries rather than tiny rapidly changing counters.
Avoid requiring frequent timed check-ins unless reminders, batching, or accessibility-friendly schedules exist.

economy.loot_table.d: A weighted reward definition that selects items, currency, upgrades, or resources from eligible entries.
p: rarity_tier: common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary
e: All entries can become ineligible after level, class, ownership, or biome filters; the table needs a fallback or explicit no-drop result.
Seeded runs must decide whether loot rolls are reproducible before or after player choices and table version changes.
Inventory limits, stack caps, duplicate_rule, and binding rules can reject a selected reward after the roll.
b: Weights are treated as percentages and expected to sum to 100 even though content edits use relative drop_weight values.
Rarity is rolled once by tier and again by item, making actual odds differ from published or intended odds.
Pity counters reset on failed eligibility checks instead of successful protected drops.
t: Balance expected reward over many rolls, not only the most exciting rare outcome.
Economy sinks, crafting inputs, and upgrade costs should be tuned against actual drop simulations.
a: Avoid relying only on color to communicate rarity; include labels, icons, sound, or sorting.
When randomness affects progression, communicate broad odds or reward pools where appropriate.

economy.repair_cost.d: A resource or currency cost paid to restore item durability, vehicle condition, equipment charges, or base structures.
e: The item is equipped, traded, destroyed, or upgraded while a repair confirmation dialog is open.
Repairing above max durability due to buffs or temporary modifiers must define the cap clearly.
A repair kit uses materials while a vendor uses coins, so failure rollback must restore the correct resource type.
b: Repair cost is calculated from displayed durability percent instead of exact durability_state, causing rounding exploits.
Transaction debits currency before validating item_instance_id ownership and loses coins on rejected repair.
Partial repair updates the UI but does not persist the new durability value to save data.
t: Repair should be noticeable enough to make damage meaningful but not so punishing that players avoid using interesting gear.
Rarity scaling needs a ceiling; otherwise high-tier equipment can become too expensive to use in ordinary content.
a: Show before/after durability, exact cost, and resource type before confirmation.
Warn clearly when a repair is partial or when repairing consumes rare materials instead of common currency.

economy.resource_conversion.d: A controlled exchange that turns one resource, currency, or material set into another at a defined rate.
e: A conversion produces fractional output and must define rounding, remainder banking, or rejection rules.
Input and output resources are both tradable, allowing circular conversion through another vendor.
Conversion limits reset by day, event, account, or save slot and need clear persistence boundaries.
b: The UI preview uses rounded values while the transaction consumes exact values and grants a different amount.
Conversion consumes input before checking output inventory capacity, losing resources on failure.
Daily limits are stored client-side and reset by clock changes or reinstalling the game.
t: Conversion ratios should usually lose some value unless the goal is explicit catch-up or accessibility smoothing.
Cap or tax routes that convert common drops into rare progression resources, or rare sinks will collapse.
a: Show input, output, fee, and remaining limit in the same confirmation view.
Offer max-convert and stepper controls that are keyboard/gamepad friendly and do not require repeated clicks.

economy.shop.d: A transaction interface where players buy, sell, or exchange items and resources through priced offers.
p: purchase_limit: 1-999 per account, run, or refresh
e: A player buys the last stock item while another client or save slot has the same shop open.
The vendor refreshes between quote and commit, invalidating offer_id or purchase_limit state.
A purchase grants an item_instance_id but inventory capacity rejects it after currency has been debited.
b: Shop UI disables a buy button based on stale wallet data and allows or blocks the wrong purchase.
Currency is debited before stock validation, so failed purchases remove coins.
Offer IDs are regenerated every refresh and old saves or pending purchases cannot reconcile them.
t: Stock limits and refresh cadence can be more important than price for controlling access to powerful items.
Shops should not sell every missing reward cheaply unless the intended role is catch-up or anti-frustration.
a: Show affordability, owned count, purchase limit, stock remaining, and item comparison without requiring fast menu navigation.
Add confirmation or undo for expensive purchases, especially when cursor focus can move during controller input.

economy.trading.d: A negotiated or direct exchange of items, resources, or currency between players, NPCs, or systems.
e: One participant disconnects after items enter escrow but before final acceptance.
An item is equipped, bound, damaged, or modified while it is shown in the trade window.
Both participants accept, then one inventory becomes full before receiving the traded item.
b: Item ownership is checked when added to the window but not rechecked when trade_session_id commits.
Accept state is not cleared after an offer changes, enabling last-second item swaps.
Currency debit succeeds for one side while item transfer fails for the other side.
t: Trading can bypass loot rarity, crafting costs, and progression gates; bind rules and level requirements should be deliberate.
Trade taxes, listing fees, or cooldowns can reduce inflation but should not make ordinary exchange feel punitive.
a: Use clear confirmation summaries that list both sides of the trade in text, including item names, quantities, and currency.
Provide enough review time and avoid accept buttons that can be triggered accidentally during offer changes.

horror.hiding.d: A defensive state where the player enters a hiding spot or concealed posture to avoid detection, searches, or chase pressure.
p: hiding_state: entering, hidden, peeking, exiting, exposed
e: The monster sees the player during the enter animation and must decide whether hiding succeeds.
The exit socket is blocked by the monster, another player, or a moved physics object.
A scripted scare or checkpoint restore occurs while the player is inside a hiding spot.
b: AI line-of-sight ignores hiding_state and detects the player through the hiding mesh.
The camera clips outside lockers or under beds during enter and peek transitions.
Exit placement pushes the player into a wall or directly into monster collision.
t: Safe hiding spots create relief; searchable hiding spots preserve tension but need readable telegraphs.
Long entry animations increase commitment and fear, but excessive lockout can feel unfair during chase sequences.
a: Support toggle or hold options for breathing, peeking, or staying hidden interactions.
Use subtitles or directional indicators for monster proximity cues that affect hiding decisions.

horror.jump_scare_trigger.d: A scripted or reactive scare event that uses timing, framing, audio, animation, and player state to create a sudden startle.
e: The player enters the trigger while already in a cutscene, menu, hiding animation, or death state.
Reduced scare mode disables audio spikes but the camera cue still snaps violently.
A scare trigger fires repeatedly because one-shot state was not persisted after reload.
b: The scare plays after the threat has been removed or the scripted actor is pooled elsewhere.
Trigger validation uses camera position instead of player state and fires through walls.
Audio and animation are not synchronized, making the scare feel broken instead of intentional.
t: Repeated jump scares lose impact quickly; pacing should leave space for anticipation and recovery.
Low-threat false alarms can teach location language, but too many make real threats feel arbitrary.
a: Provide reduced jump scare mode that lowers audio spikes, camera snaps, flash intensity, or sudden motion.
Avoid mandatory rapid input immediately after a scare unless alternate settings exist.

horror.light_resource.d: A limited-use light source that improves visibility, safety, or combat options while consuming battery, fuel, charge, or attention.
e: A refill item is used while the light source is active and draining.
The player swaps, drops, or loses the light while a monster perception modifier is active.
A checkpoint restores fuel but not the active light cone, warning band, or AI visibility state.
b: Fuel drains twice because both the item and equipped light update the same resource.
The monster AI reacts to the visual light mesh but not the authoritative light_source_id state.
Low-fuel warnings keep playing after refill because warning_band_id does not reset.
t: Low fuel should create pressure before total darkness, not instantly make navigation impossible.
Refill placement controls exploration confidence; clustered refills reduce fear while sparse refills increase route planning.
a: Offer contrast, brightness, and reduced darkness settings without removing the resource loop.
Use text, icon shape, and audio alternatives for low-fuel warnings.

horror.limited_visibility.d: A horror visibility constraint that limits what the player can see through darkness, fog, camera framing, occlusion, blindness, or unreliable light.
e: A required pickup, exit, or puzzle symbol is outside the readable visibility area.
A monster attacks from darkness before any audio or silhouette telegraph can play.
Accessibility brightness settings reveal hidden navigation blockers or stealth cues.
b: Post-processing darkness hides UI prompts, subtitles, or accessibility indicators.
AI perception uses full scene visibility while the player cannot see the same threat.
Fog and darkness settings stack multiplicatively and make the scene unreadable on some displays.
t: Darkness is more effective when the player still has enough information to choose movement, hiding, or retreat.
Visibility constraints should vary by area and pacing beat so players do not become numb to constant darkness.
a: Provide brightness, contrast, reduced vignette, and reduced blur settings.
Keep subtitles, interaction prompts, and critical UI outside heavy darkness filters.

horror.monster_patrol.d: A roaming threat behavior where a monster follows routes, reacts to perception events, investigates suspicious locations, and escalates into search or chase states.
p: monster_alert_state: patrol, suspicious, searching, chasing, returning
e: The player enters a safe room while the monster is already chasing at the boundary.
A noise lure and line-of-sight event arrive during the same AI decision step.
Navmesh updates or locked doors invalidate the current patrol route.
b: Patrol state changes are driven by animation not AI authority, causing desync between movement and decisions.
Search timeout resets every frame because suspicion never decays below the transition threshold.
The monster pathfinds to the exact player position after hearing a lure instead of the noise source.
t: Predictable patrols support planning; occasional route variation supports fear when it has readable rules.
Search behavior should punish noisy mistakes without turning every small sound into a guaranteed chase.
a: Provide subtitle, caption, or visual alternatives for monster audio cues.
Offer difficulty or assist settings that adjust search persistence and chase recovery without disabling threat identity.

horror.safe_room.d: A protected location where monsters, decay pressure, or pursuit rules are reduced so players can save, recover, manage inventory, or plan.
e: The monster reaches the doorway exactly as the player crosses the safe_room_boundary.
A scripted event temporarily disables safety and must communicate the exception clearly.
The player saves after spending resources but before storage or recovery state commits.
b: AI pathing targets a player inside the safe room and gets stuck at the boundary.
Safe room music starts but monster exclusion does not, creating contradictory cues.
Storage inventory commits independently from checkpoint data and duplicates or loses items.
t: Safe rooms should be close enough to reduce frustration but spaced to preserve route planning.
Unlimited recovery lowers fear; limited recovery or storage tradeoffs keep resource decisions meaningful.
a: Use clear audio, lighting, map labels, and text cues to identify safe-room state.
Make save and storage interactions confirmable and readable under stress.

horror.sanity_meter.d: A psychological pressure resource that changes as the player experiences darkness, threats, isolation, scripted events, or recovery sources.
e: Sanity drops below a critical threshold during a cutscene, menu, or non-interactive scare.
A recovery source and decay source overlap inside a safe room doorway or light boundary.
A hallucination spawns during combat and is mistaken for a real damage source.
b: Sanity decay continues while paused because it reads the wrong clock.
Threshold effects retrigger every frame when sanity hovers near a boundary.
Recovery applies client-side and desyncs the authoritative run or checkpoint state.
t: Sanity pressure should give players enough warning to react before severe effects begin.
Recovery sources need scarcity, placement, and readable tradeoffs so safe rooms do not erase all tension.
a: Offer reduced distortion, reduced camera movement, and lower-intensity hallucination settings.
Provide subtitle or text alternatives for audio-only sanity cues.

horror.sound_lure.d: A sound event that attracts, distracts, redirects, or escalates monster behavior based on source location, volume profile, occlusion, and AI state.
e: A lure is activated while the monster already has direct line of sight to the player.
Several noises fire at once and need deterministic priority resolution.
The lure lands somewhere reachable to the player but unreachable to the monster navmesh.
b: The monster runs to the player throw origin instead of the lure source position.
Audio playback succeeds but no noise_event_id is sent to AI perception.
Occlusion lowers the audible volume visually but not in AI logic.
t: Reliable lures empower stealth play; unreliable lures increase fear but can feel unfair without clear rules.
Consumable lures can be stronger than reusable noise sources because inventory scarcity limits abuse.
a: Provide visual indicators or subtitles for important lure sounds and monster reactions.
Avoid requiring precise audio direction alone to understand whether a lure worked.

meta.collection_log.d: An account- or profile-level record of discovered items, characters, enemies, lore entries, cosmetics, achievements, or other long-term collectibles.
p: account_id: platform or game account identifier
profile_id: local profile or save slot identifier
e: A content update renames or removes collection_entry_id values already present in old saves.
The same discovery is earned offline on two devices before cross-save conflict resolution.
A hidden spoiler entry is discovered but should not reveal locked neighboring entries.
b: Collection entries are unlocked from UI preview instead of the committed gameplay event.
Cross-save merge picks the newest profile and loses older collection entries.
Retroactive scans run every launch and repeatedly show unlock notifications.
t: Collection logs should make optional mastery visible without making normal play feel incomplete.
Hidden entries are strongest when they protect surprise, not when they obscure basic progress.
a: Provide search, filters, progress text, and clear locked-state descriptions for large logs.
Avoid communicating rarity, category, or completion only through color.

meta.daily_challenge.d: A profile-level challenge that rotates on a scheduled cadence, often using fixed modifiers, seeds, objectives, rewards, or leaderboard eligibility.
e: A player starts online, finishes offline, and reconnects after challenge_end_timestamp_ms.
Device clock differs from the server clock and shows the wrong challenge window.
The reward is claimable but the content definition changes before the claim transaction completes.
b: Daily challenge content is generated from local date and differs by time zone.
Rewards can be claimed multiple times because claim_transaction_id is not persisted before grant.
Leaderboard entries accept scores from modified clients without anti_cheat_validation.
t: Daily rewards should motivate return visits without feeling mandatory for core progression.
One-attempt dailies make leaderboards cleaner but can punish disconnects and accessibility interruptions.
a: Show start and end timestamps in local-friendly text and avoid relying on countdown color alone.
Offer readable objective summaries and allow players to review modifiers before starting.

meta.new_game_plus.d: A post-completion mode that starts a new playthrough while carrying selected account, character, item, difficulty, or completion state forward.
p: profile_id: save slot or account profile id
e: A quest item carried forward unlocks a progression gate before the world is ready.
A content update changes carryover rules for saves that already entered New Game Plus.
The migration fails after deleting old world state but before writing the new cycle.
b: Carryover copies item instances but not their upgrade, durability, or ownership metadata.
Quest flags reset visually while NPC or world scripts still read completed state.
Difficulty scaling stacks each load because ng_plus_cycle_index is reapplied repeatedly.
t: Carryover power should justify replay without trivializing early progression unless that is the promise.
Rewards need duplicate policies before launch; repeated unique items become design debt quickly.
a: Explain carryover and reset rules before the player commits to the new cycle.
Provide confirmation and backup handling for irreversible migration steps.

meta.player_profile_stats.d: Long-term account or profile statistics that summarize play history, milestones, performance, preferences, and completion across sessions.
p: account_id: platform or game account identifier
profile_id: profile slot or character profile id
e: Two devices update the same profile stat offline and later sync with different snapshots.
A stat is renamed or split during a save migration.
An achievement checks a stat before the profile transaction commits.
b: Stats increment from predicted events that later fail authoritative validation.
Cross-save merge keeps the newest snapshot and discards higher personal best records.
Profile exports include private stats despite privacy_visibility_id restrictions.
t: Stats used for matchmaking or recommendations should be resistant to farming and clearly scoped.
Public stats can motivate mastery, but overexposure can pressure players away from experimentation.
a: Let players hide or simplify public profile stats that create social pressure.
Provide searchable, sortable, and text-readable stats for large profiles.
