movement.air_dash.d: A dash that can be activated while airborne.
e: Using air dash at the exact landing frame can spend ground dash or air dash depending on priority.
Collision during hover frames must not leave gravity disabled.
Air dash into one-way platforms should not snap the player upward unexpectedly.
b: Dash charge resets repeatedly on wall contact and enables unintended climbing.
Air dash uses ground friction and loses distance immediately.
Input direction is sampled after the character flips from target lock.
t: Air dash plus double jump greatly expands reachable space and should be tested against existing levels.
Reset pickups can make air dash a route puzzle rather than a general escape option.
a: Use clear charge feedback so players know whether an air dash is available while airborne.

movement.climbing.d: A controlled movement state for ascending, descending, or moving across climbable surfaces using surface validation, snap points, stamina, and animation alignment.
e: A climbable surface can end abruptly, curve inward, or move while the character is attached.
Stamina may deplete while the player is above lethal fall height and needs a readable failure state.
Camera collision can hide the next handhold when the character is close to concave geometry.
b: Surface validation uses a forward ray only and fails when the character is slightly offset or rotated.
Root motion moves the character away from the stored surface anchor and breaks collision alignment.
Detach leaves gravity disabled or input locked after ledge transition cancellation.
t: Unlimited free climbing changes world boundary design; tagged surfaces keep routes authored and readable.
Stamina drain should reflect route length and available rest points, not only vertical distance.
a: Offer visible climbable-surface highlights or texture language instead of relying on subtle material differences.
Consider climb assists, reduced stamina drain, or forgiving ledge input buffers for long vertical routes.

movement.crouch.d: A lower movement stance that changes collision height, visibility, and available actions.
e: Uncrouching under a low ceiling must fail gracefully without camera popping through geometry.
Entering water, ladders, vehicles, or cutscenes should define whether crouch state is preserved or cleared.
Switching from crouch to slide needs one authority for collision height and momentum transfer.
b: The visual mesh stands up before the collision capsule has clearance.
Camera height changes instantly and causes motion discomfort or clipping.
Toggle crouch remains active after respawn or dialogue and traps the player in a low stance.
t: If crouch greatly reduces detection, pair it with slower movement or cover requirements.
Low tunnels should be used intentionally; repeated forced crouch corridors can feel like input tax.
a: Support both hold and toggle crouch, and store the preference separately from the binding.
Make low-clearance availability visible through level art rather than relying only on trial and error.

movement.dash.d: A short committed burst of movement in a chosen direction.
e: Dashing into a concave corner should stop or slide consistently without tunneling through thin collision.
High dash_distance over one physics step needs sweep, sub-step, or truncation rules so thin walls and small hazards are not skipped.
A buffered dash pressed before landing must choose whether to use ground rules, air rules, or be rejected.
b: Dash moves by transform position and bypasses collision sweeps, causing wall clips at low frame rates.
Recharge starts on button press instead of successful activation, rewarding invalid repeated inputs.
Dash cooldown or charge state resets after scene reload while the UI still shows the action unavailable.
t: Short recharge and long invulnerability turn dash into a primary defense; long recharge makes it a tactical escape.
If dash cancels attacks, reloads, or hit stun, it becomes part of the combat economy and should be costed there.
a: Support input buffering and consider a separate toggle for double-tap dash if repeated rapid taps are required.
Pair readiness with visual, audio, and optional haptic cues so players are not forced to track a tiny UI element.

movement.dodge_roll.d: A committed evasive movement action that briefly changes position, hit reaction rules, and recovery timing, often with invulnerability frames.
e: Roll direction should be captured at activation, not drift when lock-on target or camera heading changes mid-roll.
Incoming damage during the first or last roll frame needs consistent inclusive or exclusive immunity rules.
Rolling into stairs, ledges, or narrow doors must not leave the character inside collision after recovery.
b: Invulnerability is tied to animation events and desyncs when animation playback rate changes.
Roll hits the same hazard twice because damage immunity and hurtbox state are not updated atomically.
Input buffering triggers a roll after stun recovery even though the player released the button long ago.
t: Long i-frame windows make roll a timing solution; long displacement makes it a spacing solution.
Recovery frames are the main counterweight when roll is used in combat, especially against repeated attacks.
a: Use generous input buffering and readable attack telegraphs if roll timing is central to survival.
Consider assist settings that widen dodge_roll_i_frames_ms or reduce repeated-button strain.

movement.prone.d: A very low stance that changes collision height, movement pace, visibility, aiming profile, and the rules for standing back up.
e: A player trying to stand under a low obstacle needs a blocked stand-up state rather than collision penetration.
Weapon aiming, camera pitch, and interaction prompts may need different offsets while prone_height_multiplier is active.
Moving platforms and slopes can invalidate prone clearance after the player entered safely.
b: Capsule height changes but camera and aim origin remain at standing height.
Stand-up clearance checks ignore dynamic blockers and pop the player into another character.
Prone movement uses standing friction and slides down gentle slopes unexpectedly.
t: Prone concealment should be strong only where level geometry and AI sightlines support it.
Very slow prone pacing works for infiltration but becomes tedious if crawlspaces are long or repeated.
a: Provide toggle prone and clear blocked-stand messaging so players do not have to hold a button while crawling.
Avoid camera positions that create nausea or obscure exit visibility in tight spaces.

movement.run.d: Default higher-speed ground traversal that converts directional input into sustained travel while preserving collision, animation, camera, and prediction readability.
e: Run should not preserve full velocity when stepping from ground into a ladder, ledge grab, vehicle mount, or scripted traversal state.
Sharp input reversal near thin collision can create oscillation if deceleration and collision projection fight each other.
Camera-relative input must update correctly when lock-on, split screen, or cinematic camera changes orientation mid-run.
b: Run pace is applied directly to transform position and bypasses collision sweeps on fast frames.
Animation blend trees use raw stick magnitude and never match resolved ground velocity on slopes.
Surface material modifiers stack permanently after crossing mud, ice, or moving platforms.
t: Run pace sets the expected density of levels; increasing it may require wider lanes and earlier enemy telegraphs.
Strong acceleration feels responsive but reduces the difference between run, dash, and dodge roll.
a: Offer always-run or toggle-run options when holding a modifier would be fatiguing.
Keep camera sway, field-of-view shifts, and head bob optional or adjustable during sustained running.

movement.slide.d: A low-profile committed movement state that carries the character forward under a slide friction curve, often passing under hazards or extending momentum.
e: The player reaches slide_exit_clearance_height failure under a low ceiling and must stay crouched or prone.
Sliding from a moving platform needs parent velocity transfer without launching after detach.
Slope transitions can either accelerate, clamp, or cancel slide depending on slide_friction_curve_id.
b: Capsule height shrinks without moving the capsule center, causing feet or head collision penetration.
Slide friction is applied in render update and differs by frame rate.
Exit clearance checks ignore triggers or dynamic obstacles and stand the player inside geometry.
t: Low entry requirements make slide a default movement habit; stricter requirements make it an authored traversal tool.
Allowing attacks, reloads, or invulnerability during slide changes it from locomotion into combat defense.
a: Offer hold, toggle, or auto-slide options for games with frequent low obstacles.
Limit camera dip, motion blur, and sudden field-of-view changes, or expose comfort settings.

movement.sprint.d: High-output locomotion modifier that increases traversal pace only when extra cost, exhaustion, noise, camera, input, or recovery rules make it more than a speed multiplier.
e: Sprint input during reload, crouch, prone, ladder climb, swimming, aiming, or interaction prompts needs a clear sprint_cancel_policy_id.
Stamina exhaustion should transition to run or walk without repeatedly starting and stopping each frame.
Hold-to-sprint, toggle sprint, and auto-sprint need identical exhaustion and cancellation rules after remapping.
b: Sprint drains stamina while blocked by a wall because input is active but movement is zero.
Toggle sprint remains set after stamina exhaustion and restarts unexpectedly when stamina recovers.
Animation stride length does not match locomotion, causing foot sliding.
t: Unlimited sprint is mainly a traversal convenience; stamina sprint becomes a resource decision.
High sprint noise can make stealth routes riskier without forbidding fast movement entirely.
a: Offer hold, toggle, or auto-sprint settings to reduce sustained button pressure.
Avoid using only camera FOV changes to communicate sprint; include posture, audio, or UI state.

movement.stamina_movement.d: A locomotion layer that spends and restores stamina to gate sprinting, climbing, swimming, dodging, or other high-output movement actions.
e: Stamina can reach zero while the player is airborne, climbing, swimming, or inside an uninterruptible animation.
Pause menus, cutscenes, and dialogue need a timer_pause_policy so drain and recovery do not continue invisibly.
Save/load should restore stamina_resource and exhaustion_state without granting repeated recovery bursts.
b: Drain is applied twice because both movement state and animation event spend stamina_resource.
Regeneration starts immediately after every frame with no accepted input due to missing stamina_regen_delay_ms.
Exhaustion blocks UI, camera, or ordinary walking instead of only the intended high-output actions.
t: Shared stamina across sprint, dodge, block, and climb creates strong tradeoffs but can make one dominant action starve the others.
Regeneration delay matters as much as pool size; long delays create stop-start pacing even with large pools.
a: Offer assist settings for reduced drain, longer exhaustion warnings, or less severe lockout in traversal-heavy games.
Do not communicate low stamina only through color or controller vibration; include text, shape, or audio alternatives.

movement.swimming.d: A water locomotion state with altered control, buoyancy, visibility, and resource rules.
e: Entering water at high velocity should decide whether to preserve momentum, splash-stop, or damage the player.
Surface, ladder, ledge, and shore transitions need priority rules to avoid input traps.
Camera clipping and target lock need special handling when the water surface cuts through the view.
b: The player repeatedly enters and exits swim state at the water surface due to noisy volume overlap.
Gravity and buoyancy are both applied after the state exits, causing a sudden launch.
Oxygen continues draining in shallow water or during pause because breath state is not tied to submersion.
t: Low drag makes water a fast route; high drag makes it a hazard or puzzle medium.
Oxygen pressure should be paired with readable exits, refills, or safe pockets.
a: Use distinct visual and audio cues for oxygen warnings before damage begins.
Provide camera and motion options for underwater distortion or bobbing effects.

movement.walk.d: Baseline precision ground locomotion that turns low-intensity input into stable positioning, interaction alignment, and camera-readable movement without entering faster or committed states.
e: Tiny analog stick drift should not move character_id unless it passes walk_dead_zone_threshold and the active control scheme allows analog walking.
Digital keyboard or d-pad input needs a defined walk modifier or it becomes indistinguishable from run.
Slope, stair, and step transitions need a consistent ground_contact_state when the character crosses edges at low speed.
b: Movement uses render delta instead of fixed-step simulation and becomes inconsistent at unusual frame rates.
Acceleration resets every frame because input_vector is normalized after applying analog magnitude.
Animation blend thresholds do not match walk_pace_units_per_second, causing foot skating.
t: Walk pace defines the scale of rooms, interaction spacing, patrol avoidance, and camera comfort.
If walk is too fast, run and sprint lose identity; if too slow, basic traversal feels padded.
a: Support analog input, remappable hold-to-walk, and optional toggle-to-walk for players who cannot hold a modifier.
Avoid tying precise walking to narrow stick angles without calibration and dead-zone settings.

multiplayer.asymmetric_roles.d: Players occupy different roles with distinct abilities, permissions, information, cameras, or objective responsibilities.
p: role_id: pilot, engineer, medic, commander, infiltrator
role_assignment_seed: match seed or lobby assignment seed
e: A player disconnects while holding the only role that can open a required route or revive teammates.
A role swap happens while an ability, camera mode, or restricted interaction is already in progress.
Late joiners need a role that does not invalidate the team's current objective state.
b: Role-specific UI remains visible after a role change and exposes hidden information to the wrong player.
Server action validation checks player_id but not role_id or role_permission_policy_id.
Reconnect restores the player character but assigns the default role instead of the previous role.
t: Every role needs moments of agency; a support role should not spend most of the session waiting for others.
Powerful roles need responsibility, counterplay, or rotation rules so one player does not dominate the session.
a: Offer roles with lower mechanical intensity and roles with lower communication demands where the game supports them.
Make role responsibilities, available actions, and team dependencies visible in text, not only voice chat.

multiplayer.friendly_fire.d: Damage, healing denial, knockback, or penalties can apply when one player affects a teammate.
p: friendly_fire_rule_id: off, reduced_damage, full_damage, reflect_to_attacker, vote_punish
e: Area damage hits enemies and allies at the same tick with different team filters.
A player changes teams after firing a projectile but before it lands.
Pets, turrets, traps, or vehicles need source attribution back to the owning player.
b: Friendly fire checks current team at impact but ignores team at projectile spawn, enabling team-switch exploits.
Penalty counters increment for blocked damage or training-room hits that should be exempt.
Client-side hit markers show ally damage even though the server rejected the damage event.
t: Full team damage creates strong tactical tension but can invite griefing without penalties or private-session controls.
Reduced damage often preserves positioning awareness while avoiding accidental mission failure.
a: Provide ally outlines, hit warnings, and clear damage-source labels to reduce accidental friendly fire.
Offer non-voice forgiveness prompts and readable penalty explanations.

multiplayer.local_coop.d: Multiple players share one device, session, camera model, and input space while cooperating in the same game flow.
e: A controller disconnects while its player is holding an item, aiming, or controlling a menu.
One player joins during a boss fight, cutscene, checkpoint load, or screen transition.
Two players open inventory, dialogue, or settings panels that compete for UI focus.
b: Input is routed by device order instead of local_player_index and changes when controllers reconnect.
Guest players overwrite host settings, save data, or achievements because profile binding is implicit.
The camera teleports or zooms through walls when players separate vertically or enter different rooms.
t: Same-screen co-op encourages teamwork but needs level layouts that tolerate players moving at different skill levels.
Split screen gives independence at the cost of UI density and performance.
a: Allow each local player to remap controls, invert axes, adjust text scale, and choose assist settings independently where possible.
Provide camera and UI options that reduce motion discomfort in dynamic zoom or split-screen modes.

multiplayer.matchmaking_lobby.d: A lobby gathers players into a session, assigns slots, exposes ready state, and starts a match after authority checks succeed.
p: lobby_id: uuid or platform lobby handle
ready_state: not_ready, ready, loading, locked, failed
invite_code: 6-12 character code or platform invite token
e: The final player toggles ready while another player disconnects and the start request is already queued.
A party member joins through invite_code after the lobby filled their reserved slot with a solo player.
Host migration starts while matchmaking_ticket_id is being canceled or while map voting is unresolved.
b: Two clients are assigned the same lobby_slot_index because join requests were accepted without an atomic slot reservation.
Match start reads stale ready_state data and launches with a player still changing loadout or team.
Leaving a party cancels the wrong matchmaking_ticket_id and strands remaining players in a dead lobby.
t: Strict ready checks prevent accidental starts, but too many locks can make casual groups wait on inactive players.
Skill, region, platform, and ruleset filters should be visible enough that players understand longer search waits.
a: Expose ready state, selected map, team, and queue status through text labels as well as icons.
Support voice-free coordination with ready prompts, invite links, and clear failure messages for reconnect or privacy errors.

multiplayer.online_coop.d: Players cooperate in a shared online session where actions, state, progression, and failures must remain consistent across clients.
p: session_id: uuid or backend session handle
replicated_state_channel: movement, inventory, objectives, chat, cosmetics
e: A client reconnects after their character died, moved zones, or held a locked item transaction.
The host leaves while shared objectives, crafting queues, or base edits are mid-commit.
Predicted movement reaches a pickup first but the server grants it to another player.
b: Client-owned inventory or crafting changes are accepted without server transaction ordering.
Movement corrections restore position but not ability cooldowns, animation state, or carried objects.
Session saves serialize local client state rather than the authority snapshot and lose other players' progress.
t: Shared rewards reduce friction, while per-player rewards reduce loot conflict; both need clear UI language.
Drop-in support improves accessibility and social play, but objective scaling and enemy spawning must handle changing party size.
a: Support text chat, pings, subtitles, and non-voice coordination for players who cannot or prefer not to use voice.
Make disconnect, reconnect, and migration states visible so players understand whether progress is safe.

multiplayer.ping_system.d: Players place contextual markers, callouts, or alerts that communicate location and intent without requiring voice chat.
p: ping_category_id: danger, loot, defend, regroup, enemy_seen
e: A ping targets an enemy, door, or loot item that despawns before teammates receive the marker.
A muted or blocked player sends pings that should be hidden for some teammates but not the whole squad.
Rapid pings are rate-limited while an urgent downed or danger ping should still get through.
b: Pings attach to world coordinates but not moving targets, causing enemy markers to lag behind or reveal stale positions.
Rate limiting is local-only and can be bypassed by direct network requests.
Map pings and world pings use different category ids and show inconsistent icons.
t: Low friction pings improve coordination, but unlimited pings quickly drown out important callouts.
Enemy pings may need decay, uncertainty, or line-of-sight rules to avoid becoming wallhacks.
a: Pings should include visual icons, text labels, audio cues, and optional subtitles so they are not voice-dependent.
Allow players to mute, reduce, or filter ping categories without losing critical objective or danger alerts.

multiplayer.revive_teammate.d: A player restores a downed teammate through a channel, interaction, item, or protected rescue sequence.
e: Two teammates revive the same target and one cancels while the other should continue.
The downed player disconnects, bleeds out, or changes teams during the revive channel.
The reviver loses line of sight or moves out of interaction radius due to knockback or platform motion.
b: Revive progress is owned by the client and can be completed after the target is no longer downed.
Animation starts on both players at different ticks and the target snaps or stands early.
Post-revive invulnerability applies to all damage sources, including hazards that should remain dangerous.
t: Long channels create rescue tension, but they require enough cover, crowd control, or revive tools to feel fair.
Invulnerability should prevent spawn-kill frustration without letting revived players safely attack for free.
a: Offer hold, toggle, or repeated-press revive input options for players with different motor needs.
Show downed timers, interruption causes, and revive progress through text and icons, not only radial fills.

multiplayer.role_swap.d: Players exchange roles, seats, characters, or responsibilities under validated session rules.
e: A swap request is accepted while one player is dead, disconnected, stunned, or in a non-interruptible action.
Role UI changes before the server commits permissions and lets a player issue invalid commands.
A vehicle or station seat changes owner while physics, camera, or input prediction is mid-update.
b: Only client UI swaps roles while server-side permission checks still use the old role_id.
Active cooldowns, inventory locks, or objective ownership are copied twice or lost during transfer.
Two swap requests commit in the same tick and leave a player with no role or two roles.
t: Role swapping improves flexibility, but unrestricted swaps can bypass role weaknesses or encounter constraints.
Mutual confirmation prevents accidental griefing, while emergency takeover rules help when a player disconnects.
a: Allow role handoff for players who need a lower-intensity task during difficult sequences.
Show swap requests, consequences, and confirmation states in text so voice chat is not required.

multiplayer.shared_resource_pool.d: Multiple players contribute to and spend from a shared pool of currency, materials, charges, or objective resources.
e: Two players spend the last available resource units on different upgrades during the same server tick.
A player disconnects after reserving resources but before the target craft, vote, or upgrade completes.
A party member leaves and the game must decide whether their contributions stay with the team.
b: Clients subtract shared resources locally and later receive a server correction that makes UI totals jump backward.
Failed spend requests do not release reserved resources, permanently reducing the visible pool.
Contribution logs use display names instead of player_id and cannot survive renames or reconnects.
t: Shared pools reduce individual hoarding but can create social friction if spending rights are unclear.
Large purchases benefit from confirmation, vote, or role restrictions so one player cannot erase group progress.
a: Show pool changes with readable text, contribution source, and spend reason for players who miss transient notifications.
Provide non-voice approval flows for vote-required spending.

multiplayer.team_objective.d: A shared objective tracks team progress, contributions, completion rules, and rewards under authoritative scoring.
p: objective_state_id: inactive, active, contested, complete, failed
e: A player switches teams or disconnects after contributing but before rewards are distributed.
Two teams complete opposing objective conditions on the same server tick.
Late joiners enter after objective progress crossed a reward threshold.
b: Objective completion is calculated on each client and produces split-brain success or failure states.
Contribution logs are reset on host migration and players lose credit.
Team rewards can be claimed twice by reconnecting with a new player record.
t: Objectives should reward non-damage roles such as defense, revives, resource delivery, and communication when those roles matter.
Contribution thresholds can prevent freeloading, but they should not punish support players whose impact is indirect.
a: Show objective status, contribution requirements, and failure reasons through text and persistent HUD elements.
Support ping and non-voice callouts for objective changes, especially when roles have different viewpoints.

narrative.branching_dialogue.d: A conversation system where player choices, dialogue nodes, conditions, and results move narrative state through authored branches.
e: A choice becomes invalid while the conversation is open because quest_stage_id or inventory state changes.
Voice playback, subtitle events, and choice UI must stay synchronized after skip, pause, or language change.
Multiplayer conversations need a policy for which player owns the choice and how others see it.
b: Choice history records display text instead of dialogue_choice_id, breaking localization and save migration.
Branch conditions are checked for display but not rechecked when the player confirms the choice.
Voice line ids and subtitle_event_id records drift after editing dialogue timing.
t: High-impact choices need enough context that players understand the kind of consequence they are accepting.
Hidden conditions add depth, but too many invisible locked options make dialogue feel arbitrary.
a: Support readable text scaling, subtitle settings, pauseable dialogue, and optional choice timeout extensions.
Do not require players to process voiced dialogue without captions, speaker labels, and conversation logs.

narrative.codex_journal.d: A persistent lore, quest, or reference log that unlocks entries, tracks read state, and gives players a structured way to revisit narrative information.
p: discovery_trigger_id: pickup, dialogue, quest_stage, scan, area_enter
journal_sort_key: recent, category, faction, quest, region
e: A codex entry is discovered before the player reaches the chapter where its full text is spoiler-safe.
An entry is updated by later dialogue and must preserve read state while marking new paragraphs unread.
Localization changes text length enough to affect sorting, search snippets, or page layout.
b: Unlock triggers fire repeatedly and spam journal notifications after reload.
Read/unread state is stored per UI tab instead of per codex_entry_id.
Search indexes source text but not localized strings, so search fails in non-default languages.
t: Critical quest guidance should be clearly separated from optional lore so players can find required information quickly.
Frequent notifications can train players to ignore the journal; reserve strong alerts for meaningful updates.
a: Support text scaling, contrast, screen-reader-friendly structure where applicable, and controller/keyboard navigation.
Offer audio replay or captioned transcript links when entries summarize voiced discoveries.

narrative.environmental_storytelling.d: Narrative information delivered through placed objects, spaces, lighting, sound, bodies, props, or level composition rather than direct exposition.
p: authored_clue_id: blood trail, broken_lock, photo, graffiti
e: Physics objects can move, break, or despawn before the player sees a required clue.
A lighting or camera pass can make the authored clue unreadable from normal player routes.
Quest state can change the meaning of a clue, requiring updated inspect text or spoiler gates.
b: Discovery trigger fires through walls or floors because proximity checks ignore line of sight.
Clue placement works in editor but becomes hidden behind dynamic objects, weather, or NPC crowds.
Journal unlocks use scene object names instead of stable authored_clue_id records.
t: Optional environmental clues can be subtle; required clues need redundancy through layout, lighting, interaction prompts, or journal fallback.
Too many inspectable props reduce trust that any single clue matters.
a: Offer inspect prompts, high-contrast clue highlighting, captions for ambient story audio, and journal summaries for discovered clues.
Do not rely only on tiny prop details, color, or spatial audio for required story comprehension.

narrative.reputation_choice.d: A narrative choice that changes faction standing, relationship state, or social trust and can trigger immediate or delayed consequences.
p: reputation_threshold_id: hostile, wary, neutral, trusted, allied
e: A choice affects multiple factions with opposing reputation changes and delayed events.
The same conversation can be replayed after a save load and must not grant reputation twice.
A player makes a choice offline or in co-op where another player owns the narrative profile.
b: Reputation points are changed for UI preview and then committed again on confirmation.
Delayed consequence events fire after the faction or quest line has been removed by another branch.
Choice history records node order rather than stable choice_commit_id values.
t: Large reputation swings should be tied to choices with enough context and consequence framing.
Hidden reputation can add role-playing texture, but players need enough feedback to understand social systems.
a: Use clear text explanations and reviewable choice logs for players who need more time to process consequences.
Avoid using only color, tone of voice, or subtle facial animation to communicate reputation changes.

narrative.reputation_gating.d: A narrative or systemic access rule that unlocks, hides, alters, or blocks content based on faction standing, relationship state, or social trust.
p: reputation_faction_id: canonical faction or relationship id
bypass_condition_ids: item, disguise, quest flag, skill, bribe
e: Players can belong to hostile factions with conflicting gates and bypass conditions.
Temporary disguises, bribes, or story states may override reputation without changing the underlying standing.
Content patches can move thresholds and affect existing saves in the middle of a quest line.
b: UI hides a locked option without explaining the reputation requirement or alternate route.
Negative reputation uses the wrong faction key after save migration.
Bypass conditions unlock content but do not set required world_state_flag_id records.
t: Hard gates make choices consequential but can hide too much content if no alternate route exists.
Soft gates with bypasses preserve agency while still honoring reputation history.
a: Explain locked options in plain language and avoid color-only faction standing indicators.
Keep reputation summaries readable in journals or dialogue logs so players can review why a gate changed.

physics.breakable_object.d: A prop or small object changes state, spawns pieces, drops rewards, or disappears after sufficient impact or damage.
e: Multiple hits arrive in the same frame and try to spawn debris or rewards more than once.
A pooled prop is reused but still has old damage, broken visuals, or disabled collision.
A breakable object is saved while mid-break animation or while debris is still interactive.
b: The object disables its collider before the hit transaction finishes, so loot spawns at an invalid position.
Client and server both spawn rewards because break authority is not centralized.
Debris pieces use the same collision layer as the intact prop and block narrow routes after breaking.
t: Fragile props encourage experimentation, but too many loot-bearing objects can slow pacing as players smash everything.
Break thresholds should match visual material; ceramic, wood, metal, and stone should not all react identically.
a: Use distinct silhouettes, material cues, or interaction prompts so breakable props are not identified only by subtle cracks.
Avoid requiring rapid repeated hits on breakables unless an alternate input or hold option exists.

physics.buoyancy.d: Objects and characters react to fluid volumes by floating, sinking, bobbing, or resisting motion based on submerged state.
e: An object is partly inside two overlapping fluid volumes with different density or damage rules.
A sleeping rigidbody enters fluid due to moving water, streaming, or a rising flood volume.
A player exits the water while the camera, audio filter, and movement controller still think they are submerged.
b: Buoyancy pushes upward from the center of mass only, causing long objects to float unrealistically or flip violently.
Drag is applied every render frame instead of fixed step and changes with frame rate.
Submerged state toggles rapidly at the waterline, spamming splash effects and movement mode changes.
t: High drag makes water feel heavy and readable but can frustrate traversal if the player has little control authority.
Puzzle objects should have visually learnable density classes so players do not need trial and error for every item.
a: Provide stable camera options and reduced bobbing for players sensitive to waterline motion.
Use audio, particle, and UI state changes in addition to color shifts for submerged or drowning states.

physics.destructible_environment.d: Parts of the level can be damaged, fractured, removed, or converted into debris that changes navigation and tactics.
e: Destroying a bridge, wall, or floor removes the only route to a required objective or spawn point.
A navmesh rebuild occurs while AI agents are pathing through the damaged area.
A late-joining client needs the exact destruction state without replaying every historical damage event.
b: Destroyed chunk state is not saved, so reload restores blocked paths or duplicate rewards.
Damage is applied to child debris after fracture and recursively creates far more bodies than the performance budget allows.
Clients predict different fracture results because random chunk ordering or floating-point impulses are not deterministic.
t: Destruction is most satisfying when it opens options, but critical paths need fallback routes or repair rules.
Debris damage, cover removal, and visibility changes can swing combat difficulty more than the initial explosion.
a: Provide reduced debris, reduced camera shake, and reduced particle options for destruction-heavy scenes.
Use shape, silhouette, and UI cues to distinguish destructible surfaces from purely decorative damage.

physics.gravity.d: A persistent acceleration field pulls bodies along a defined vector and shapes jumps, falls, arcs, and physical weight.
e: A body crosses from world gravity into a local field while airborne and keeps stale terminal velocity settings.
A jump, knockback, or dash overrides vertical velocity during the same fixed step that gravity is integrated.
Large frame spikes cause multiple fixed steps and make fall damage or landing events fire more than once.
b: Gravity is applied in both Update and the fixed simulation loop, doubling fall acceleration on high frame rates.
Character controllers and rigidbodies use different gravity_scale_multiplier values and separate jump tuning tables.
Terminal velocity clamps upward motion as well as falling motion because the velocity sign is not checked.
t: Stronger gravity can make jumps feel crisp, but it narrows correction windows for players with slower reactions.
Terminal velocity should match level scale and fall recovery; very high caps make pits feel punitive and collision tunneling more likely.
a: Offer assists such as wider coyote windows, jump buffering, or reduced fall penalty when gravity tuning demands fast reactions.
Use clear environmental cues for altered gravity fields so players are not surprised by sudden motion changes.

physics.low_gravity_zone.d: A volume or region reduces gravity effects for selected bodies, changing jump arcs, falling, and object motion.
e: A player straddles the boundary with the character center outside but feet or projectiles inside.
Multiple zones overlap and disagree about priority, blend windows, or affected body classes.
A saved game loads with bodies inside the zone before trigger enter events have fired.
b: Gravity multiplier is applied cumulatively every frame instead of replacing or blending from the base field.
Leaving the zone snaps vertical velocity and causes sudden fall damage or ceiling collisions.
Projectiles and characters use different active zone ids, so aiming previews do not match actual arcs.
t: Lower multipliers widen jump and reaction windows but can make hazards too easy unless level scale adapts.
Boundaries should be placed where players can safely test the altered arc before facing punishment.
a: Provide visual boundary cues and optional UI state so players know when altered gravity is active.
Reduce camera bob or auto-tilt in low gravity areas if floaty motion causes discomfort.

physics.moving_platform.d: A surface moves through the world while transferring some or all of its motion to passengers standing on it.
p: platform_velocity_vector: 0.5-20 world units per second along route
e: The platform reverses direction while a passenger is partly off the edge or touching a wall.
A rider jumps on the same fixed step that the platform changes route node or teleports to a reset pose.
Parenting a character to a rotating platform changes input axes, camera assumptions, or interpolation order.
b: Passenger velocity is applied twice: once through transform parenting and once through character movement.
Fast downward platforms leave riders behind because contact is lost before transfer occurs.
Moving platforms crush characters against ceilings without a clear damage, stop, or push-out rule.
t: Platform routes should telegraph start, stop, and reversal points early enough for players to plan jumps.
Fast platforms create excitement but reduce accessibility unless detach grace, coyote windows, and camera framing support them.
a: Avoid requiring blind jumps from moving platforms; use framing, route previews, or repeatable rhythms.
Provide wider timing windows or alternate routes when moving platforms combine with instant-fail hazards.

physics.one_way_platform.d: A platform blocks movement from selected approach directions while allowing entry or exit through other directions.
e: Fast upward movement must not snag on the platform underside or become a false landing after tunneling.
A moving one-way platform changes contact normals while carrying the player sideways or downward.
Characters spawn or load inside the platform and need a recovery rule before collision becomes solid.
b: Collision toggles globally and makes the platform non-solid for every actor instead of only the dropping actor.
Previous-frame position is sampled after movement, so the approach-side test always thinks the actor came from above.
Drop-through re-enables before the actor clears platform thickness and catches them in a loop.
t: Dense one-way layouts support vertical combat but can become visually confusing without consistent platform art.
Drop-through delay should be long enough to avoid re-catching but short enough to allow quick recovery.
a: Use consistent visual language for semisolid platforms so players can identify collision behavior before jumping.
Allow remappable or hold-based drop-through input for players who have difficulty pressing down plus jump quickly.

physics.pendulum_swing.d: A body swings around an anchor through a constraint, rope, chain, or joint while conserving and redirecting momentum.
p: joint_anchor: world position or body-local anchor point
tangential_input_acceleration: 0-80 world units per second squared
e: The rope anchor moves, despawns, or becomes blocked while the player is attached.
The swinging body collides with walls or ceilings and the constraint solver injects unexpected energy.
Release occurs during a rollback correction, leaving client and server with different outgoing velocity.
b: Input acceleration is applied in world axes instead of along the tangent, so pumping feels inconsistent.
Constraint length changes after collision correction and slowly stretches or shrinks the rope.
Release impulse uses the previous frame velocity and drops momentum at low frame rates.
t: Longer ropes create slower, wider arcs; shorter ropes demand faster release timing and tighter camera framing.
High input acceleration gives players control but can erase the pendulum feel if they can steer directly.
a: Provide generous attach windows, buffered release, or alternate routes when swing timing is mandatory.
Reduce camera roll or auto-camera lag during large arcs for players sensitive to sweeping motion.

physics.physics_push_pull.d: Players move physical objects by pushing, pulling, grabbing, or dragging them through collision-aware interaction.
p: grip_anchor_offset: body-local offset near handle or face center
push_acceleration: 0.5-20 world units per second squared
e: The object wedges against a corner while the player remains locked to the manipulation state.
A moving platform, elevator, or slope changes the object frame of reference during push or pull.
Two players or AI actors attempt to manipulate the same body from different anchors.
b: The player capsule overlaps the object after release and is pushed through walls by collision correction.
Client prediction moves the object locally but the server rejects the manipulation because mass or ownership changed.
Push acceleration ignores object mass and makes small props and heavy blocks move identically.
t: Manipulation pace should respect object weight without forcing long, repetitive pushes across empty rooms.
Grid-based pushing is easier to read for puzzles; freeform physics allows more emergence but needs stronger recovery tools.
a: Offer hold-to-push, toggle-grab, or simplified alignment options for players who struggle with sustained inputs.
Use clear object highlights and invalid-movement cues so players can understand why a push or pull is blocked.

physics.ragdoll.d: A character skeleton transitions from authored animation to simulated rigid bodies connected by joint constraints.
e: A character ragdolls while attached to a ladder, vehicle, moving platform, or cinematic root-motion track.
The body falls asleep inside a door, elevator, or other moving collision volume.
A get-up attempt begins when the pelvis is off navmesh or the selected pose intersects geometry.
b: Animation keeps writing bone transforms after physics simulation starts, causing jitter or exploding joints.
Collision layers let limbs collide with the owning capsule or weapon and launch the body.
Joint constraints are too loose or solver iterations too low, producing stretching, spinning, or folded bodies.
t: Long ragdoll recovery removes player agency; use it deliberately for heavy hits or readable punishment.
Combat readability often benefits from capped impact impulses so bodies do not obscure targets or objectives.
a: Offer reduced ragdoll intensity or less exaggerated impacts for players sensitive to violent body motion.
Keep critical gameplay information independent from ragdoll pose, since bodies may settle unpredictably.

physics.wind_force.d: An environmental air current modifies movement for characters, projectiles, particles, vehicles, or loose objects.
p: gust_acceleration_vector: 0-60 world units per second squared
affected_layer_mask: player, glider, arrows, debris, particles
e: A projectile preview ignores wind while the fired projectile is affected by the gust field.
Wind pushes the player into a wall or hazard and collision correction amplifies the sideways motion.
Overlapping gust volumes produce abrupt direction changes because priority or blending is undefined.
b: Wind is applied every render frame instead of fixed step, changing displacement by frame rate.
Affected layer masks include heavy static props and wake too many sleeping bodies at once.
Turbulence noise is sampled nondeterministically and desyncs replay or multiplayer projectile paths.
t: Strong gusts should be paired with visible wind direction, safe test spaces, or recovery routes.
Wind that affects projectiles can deepen aiming, but it should not make short-range combat feel random.
a: Use readable particle direction, sound, and environment motion rather than relying only on subtle cloth or grass animation.
Offer reduced particle density or motion intensity while preserving gameplay-readable wind indicators.

platforming.coyote_time.d: A short grace window that allows jumping shortly after leaving a valid floor.
e: Walking off a moving platform should preserve or discard the platform velocity by design.
Damage knockback off a ledge should not always grant a free recovery jump.
Leaving one-way platforms, slopes, or crumbling floors needs eligibility rules.
b: Grace timer refreshes while touching wall collision that is not a floor.
The timer uses render frames and varies with frame rate.
Jump buffering and coyote time both consume input and produce two jumps.
t: Long grace windows make ledges forgiving but can blur into an extra air jump.
Hard precision games may expose grace as an assist setting rather than defaulting to a large window.
a: Coyote time is an effective motor accessibility affordance when platforming demands frequent edge jumps.

platforming.double_jump.d: An additional jump that can be triggered after leaving the ground.
e: Walking off a ledge after a grounded jump must not accidentally consume the extra jump unless the design wants it.
Landing on moving platforms, enemies, water, or one-way platforms must reset jump counters consistently.
Buffered jump input during knockback or ledge grab should not spend an air jump after control returns.
b: Extra jump resets every frame while touching wall collision because wall contact is treated as ground.
The second jump stacks with downward velocity and feels too weak after falling for a long distance.
Animation state reports grounded early and grants an unintended third jump.
t: High vertical impulse turns double jump into a route unlock; low impulse makes it mainly a correction tool.
Resetting downward momentum is more forgiving than additive impulse and should be considered in hazard spacing.
a: Combine with jump buffering and coyote time when the game expects frequent precise air jumps.
Use a distinct sound or animation for the spent air jump so players can track remaining jumps without reading UI.

platforming.drop_through_platform.d: An intentional input that lets the player fall through an eligible platform.
e: Drop input while crouched, attacking, or stunned should not accidentally fire.
Dropping through a moving platform should preserve expected relative motion.
Stacked platforms need a rule for whether one input drops through one or many layers.
b: Collision is disabled for all platforms instead of only the current platform.
The player immediately lands again because collision returns before clearing thickness.
Input buffering turns a normal landing jump into an unintended drop.
t: Fast drop-through supports arena flow; strict input chords reduce accidental falls in precision layouts.
Hazards beneath platforms should be telegraphed if drop-through is common.
a: Allow remapping the drop input and avoid requiring awkward simultaneous inputs on small controllers.

platforming.jump_buffering.d: A short input buffer that stores a jump press just before jumping becomes legal.
e: Buffered jump during hit stun, ladder attach, ledge climb, or other animation locks should usually expire before control returns.
Cutscenes, dialogue choices, pause menus, and UI focus changes must clear or suspend the buffer so a stale jump does not fire after control resumes.
Landing, coyote time, wall contact, and double-jump eligibility can become true in the same simulation tick and need a deterministic priority order.
b: The buffer never clears after an invalid jump and fires seconds later.
Hold-to-jump creates repeated buffered jumps every frame.
The buffer consumes input before variable jump height can read button release.
t: A small buffer improves feel without changing challenge; a large buffer can make rhythmic timing automatic.
Buffering should be tested with coyote time because the pair changes perceived jump leniency.
a: Expose stronger buffering in assist settings for games with frequent precision jumps.

platforming.ledge_climb.d: A recovery transition that moves a hanging character onto the top of a ledge using clearance checks, animation alignment, and collision restoration.
e: The top landing area becomes blocked after the player starts climbing.
Damage, knockback, or a scripted event interrupts during root motion and must restore collision safely.
Moving ledges require exit offset relative to moving_platform_id rather than a world point.
b: Collision is disabled for the animation and never restored after cancel.
Root motion moves through the wall because no sweep validates the climb path.
Top clearance uses standing height even when the intended exit is crouched under an obstacle.
t: Long climb animations create vulnerability and tension; short climbs make ledge recovery nearly automatic.
Combat encounters near ledges need clear rules for whether climbing grants protection or vulnerability.
a: Allow buffered climb input from hang state and avoid requiring rapid repeated presses to recover.
Use camera framing and prompts that remain readable while the character is hanging.

platforming.ledge_grab.d: A platforming recovery state that detects a ledge, validates clearance, snaps the character to a hang point, and waits for climb, drop, or jump input.
e: The ledge is detected but top clearance is blocked by a moving crate, enemy, or closing door.
A player can approach the same edge from jump, wall slide, climb, or knockback states with different priorities.
Moving platforms need ledge_id and snap position stored relative to platform transform.
b: Detection rays catch decorative trim that has no safe hang or climb position.
Character snaps through the ledge because clearance is checked after changing position.
Hang state disables gravity but never restores it when drop input is buffered.
t: Automatic ledge grab increases forgiveness but can interrupt intentional falls or speed routes.
Grip stamina adds tension but should not punish players while they are reading the next safe input.
a: Provide optional auto-grab, input buffering, and visible ledge affordances for precision-heavy sections.
Avoid making required ledges distinguishable only by tiny geometry differences.

platforming.variable_jump_height.d: A jump model where release timing changes apex height by cutting upward velocity, changing gravity, or limiting sustained impulse.
e: Jump release can arrive before the physics tick that consumes buffered jump input.
Coyote time and jump buffering can overlap and must not create two jumps from one press.
Head collision during held jump should cut upward velocity and clear held-jump extension.
b: Jump release is read in render update and produces different arcs by frame rate.
Holding jump through a landing immediately triggers another full-height jump unintentionally.
Apex gravity multiplier stacks with low-gravity zones and creates floaty or infinite arcs.
t: Wide hold windows are forgiving but can make short hops harder unless release cutoff is strong.
Fast fall multipliers make jumps snappy but reduce reaction time for landing corrections.
a: Offer input buffering and optional wider jump hold windows for precision-heavy games.
Avoid requiring extremely short taps for required routes unless assist settings or alternate paths exist.

platforming.wall_jump.d: A jump launched from contact with a wall or steep vertical surface.
e: Inside corners can report two wall normals; choose the jump normal deterministically.
Moving, rotating, or crumbling walls must specify whether momentum is inherited.
Buffered jump after wall slide must not also trigger ground jump when the player lands during the buffer.
b: The wall normal is taken from the wrong contact point, launching the player into the wall.
Wall contact remains true for one extra physics step and grants jumps in open air.
Same-wall lockout prevents valid jumps on closely spaced opposite walls because contact IDs are reused.
t: High horizontal impulse favors fast rebounds; low impulse favors controlled climbing and precision.
Generous contact grace makes wall jump approachable, but too much grace lets players jump from walls they no longer perceive.
a: Use surface marking, character pose, or controller vibration to show when a wall jump is available.
Avoid requiring simultaneous opposite-direction and jump inputs unless alternate input options exist.

platforming.wall_slide.d: A controlled descent state that slows the character while touching a wall.
e: A player pressing into a wall at the top of a ledge should not get trapped between ledge grab and slide.
Wall slide on moving platforms must decide whether lateral movement is inherited.
Contact with decorative or one-way surfaces needs explicit slide eligibility.
b: The slide state flickers because wall contact is lost for one frame on tile seams.
Downward velocity cap is applied after gravity and creates frame-rate dependent descent.
Players can slide upward when pushed by moving walls because the cap only handles falling.
t: Lower descent caps make vertical routes safer; higher caps keep wall slide as a brief recovery affordance.
If wall slide feeds wall jump, tune both together so the slide does not trivialize timing.
a: Consider a hold-to-cling option for players who need more time to plan wall jumps.
Show valid slide surfaces through material language or consistent character pose.

procedural_generation.biome_generation.d: A region and content-distribution generator that assigns biome identities, boundaries, environment rules, resources, hazards, encounter pools, and visual themes across a map or world.
p: biome_id: forest, desert, tundra, swamp, volcanic
e: A required resource appears only in a biome that the seed failed to place near reachable progression routes.
Biome transitions create narrow hazard strips, visual seams, or mismatched collision/navigation rules.
Adjacent biome rules reject every candidate and require fallback_template_id or repair passes.
b: Biome masks use different coordinates than terrain chunks, causing decoration and ground textures to disagree.
Resource placement samples biome_id before transition blending and spawns desert resources in forest visuals.
RNG stream sharing means adding a new biome changes loot or encounter generation elsewhere.
t: Biome size should support travel goals: tiny regions feel noisy, while huge regions can starve players of needed resources.
Resource density and enemy difficulty need to be tuned per biome so visual variety also affects play.
a: Use shapes, landmarks, labels, and material changes in addition to color to distinguish biome boundaries.
Avoid dense procedural decoration that hides hazards, enemies, or interactables without visibility options.

procedural_generation.loot_generation.d: A procedural reward process that selects, rolls, filters, and grants loot from tables, context, rarity, and player state.
p: rarity_tier: common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary
e: The selected item cannot be granted because inventory is full, item definition is missing, or duplicate_rule rejects it.
A deterministic run needs loot rolls to reproduce even when optional containers are skipped.
Player level, biome_id, and quest flags filter out every table entry.
b: Loot rolls happen on both client and server and grant two different rewards.
Duplicate conversion grants currency but does not suppress the original item_instance_id.
Rarity filters are applied after item selection, making published odds inaccurate.
t: Balance expected value over many rolls and track actual drop distributions by loot_table_id.
Smart loot improves relevance but can reduce excitement if every reward is too predictable.
a: Show reward names, rarity labels, and duplicate conversion results in text as well as color or animation.
Allow reveal animations to be skipped, paused, or reduced for repeated loot drops.

procedural_generation.procedural_level_r.d: A room-selection and placement generator that instantiates authored or parameterized room templates into a validated layout with sockets, collision checks, and fallback rules.
e: A required doorway socket is blocked by props, hazards, or collision after decoration.
The room pool runs out of templates matching the needed size, tag, or critical path role.
A lock room appears before the key room or ability unlock that opens it.
b: Rooms align visually but their navigation meshes, collision, or door triggers do not connect.
Template IDs are selected by array index, so adding a room changes old seeds unpredictably.
Validation checks only room graph connectivity and misses actual unreachable areas after decoration.
t: Room pool variety should be tuned against session length; too few templates expose repetition quickly.
Critical path rooms should teach mechanics and scale risk before optional branches add complexity.
a: Ensure generated room readability with landmarks, exits, and map support rather than relying on memorized layouts.
Avoid narrow procedural routes that require precision movement unless the game clearly supports it.

procedural_generation.procedural_quests.d: A system that assembles quest objectives, targets, locations, rewards, and text from templates and world state.
p: quest_template_id: fetch, hunt, escort, delivery, investigate
e: Generated target_id is killed, looted, moved, or despawned before the quest is accepted or completed.
Objective order sends players through locked areas, missing traversal abilities, or invalid biomes.
Generated text references a faction, item, or location that validation later replaces.
b: Quest generator validates location reachability but not whether the required item or NPC can spawn there.
Template variables are replaced in UI text but not in tracking markers or save data.
validation_retries eventually accept a quest with missing objective_node_id because fallback checks are weaker.
t: Procedural quests need caps and cooldowns so generated chores do not overwhelm authored goals.
Reward value should account for travel distance, risk, required items, and expected time.
a: Quest text should clearly name target, location, reward, and next step; avoid vague generated phrasing.
Markers, logs, and map filters should support players who cannot memorize generated names or routes.

procedural_generation.procedural_terrain.d: A generation system that builds playable landforms, chunks, surfaces, or height fields from seeds, noise, biome rules, and validation passes.
p: chunk_coordinate: integer x,z or x,y chunk coordinate
e: Spawn positions can appear inside water, cliffs, caves, or unreachable terrain unless validated against traversal rules.
Chunk boundaries must align height, collision, resources, roads, rivers, and nav data without visible seams.
Changing generation rules after release can break existing world seeds, saved bases, or player-made structures.
b: Visual mesh and collision mesh are generated from different samples and no longer line up.
Biome blending creates thin invalid strips that trap players or pathfinding agents.
Generation runs on the render thread and stalls when the player crosses chunk boundaries.
t: Terrain variety should serve navigation and goals; pure noise often creates fatigue rather than exploration.
Resource, enemy, and landmark placement need to be balanced against terrain difficulty and travel cost.
a: Avoid relying only on subtle color changes to distinguish traversal-safe terrain from hazards.
Provide map, marker, or pathing support if generated terrain can create visually dense navigation problems.

procedural_generation.random_encounters.d: A generation system that selects and places encounter content such as enemies, events, hazards, or rewards from contextual rules.
p: encounter_tag_filter: biome, faction, difficulty, story tags
e: All eligible encounter templates fail because player progression, biome, and safe spawn rules conflict.
An encounter spawns behind a one-way gate or inside a cleared safe zone.
Cooldowns and story flags can block every event in a small region.
b: Encounter selection ignores current biome_id and spawns enemies that cannot navigate the terrain.
Rejection reasons are not logged, making empty travel segments impossible to tune.
Random encounters repeat because cooldown_group_id is saved per scene instead of per world/account scope.
t: Encounter frequency should respect recovery resources and travel distance, not only enemy difficulty.
Surprise encounters need fairness constraints such as sightline, warning, or escape space.
a: Avoid unavoidable surprise attacks without warning cues, especially from behind the camera.
Offer difficulty or assist options that adjust encounter_budget and frequency rather than only health values.

procedural_generation.room_connection_gr.d: A topology generator that defines rooms as graph nodes and doorways, corridors, locks, keys, exits, or transitions as validated graph edges before room content is placed.
e: A lock appears before its key or ability gate, causing a soft-lock.
Doorway sockets selected by room_template_id do not physically align even though the graph edge exists.
Optional branches consume all valid room templates and leave no fallback for the critical path.
b: Connectivity validation checks graph edges but not actual spawned doorway collisions or navmesh reachability.
Random graph traversal uses unordered sets and produces different topology from the same seed.
Dead-end treasure rooms are selected for mandatory objectives because room tags are too broad.
t: Critical path length drives session duration more reliably than total room count.
Loops reduce backtracking frustration but can weaken lock/key or chase pacing if overused.
a: Generated maps should represent graph structure clearly when navigation complexity is high.
Avoid procedurally creating maze-like graphs without landmarks, map tools, or pathfinding support.

procedural_generation.seeded_generation.d: A deterministic generation approach where a seed and content version reproduce the same generated result under the same rules.
e: Changing content_version can make old seeds produce different maps unless old rules are retained or migrated.
Parallel generation consumes RNG streams in nondeterministic order unless each chunk or subsystem has its own rng_stream_id.
A validation retry can accidentally consume extra random values and desync later generation.
b: Loot generation consumes from the terrain RNG stream and changes the world when an item table is edited.
Seeded bug reports omit content_version, so developers cannot reproduce the player's map.
Save files store only generated output and lose the generation_seed needed to rebuild missing chunks.
t: Separate streams let designers tune loot, terrain, and encounters independently without invalidating every seed.
Daily or challenge seeds should lock content_version so leaderboards are not affected by mid-event patches.
a: Expose seed text in a copyable field so players can share and report worlds accurately.
For challenge seeds, disclose major rule modifiers so players are not surprised by hidden generation constraints.

procedural_generation.wave_generation.d: A procedural pacing system that builds timed enemy or challenge waves from budgets, spawn groups, difficulty curves, and validation rules.
e: Spawn validation rejects all candidates because the arena is full, blocked, or visible to the player.
A previous wave has stuck enemies, summons, or offscreen units that prevent wave completion.
Difficulty scaling outpaces resource drops and creates unwinnable attrition.
b: Wave completion checks only spawned count and ignores enemies converted, despawned, or stuck outside the arena.
Budget rounding always favors cheap enemies and never selects elites.
Spawn groups are selected client-side and desync in networked co-op.
t: Wave intensity should be tuned through spawn timing, composition, and recovery windows, not only enemy health.
Use telemetry for time-to-clear, damage taken, and resource remaining to tune difficulty_curve_id.
a: Provide clear wave counters, preparation cues, and remaining-enemy indicators when waves gate progress.
Allow reduced intensity or longer inter-wave cooldowns in accessibility or difficulty settings.

progression.achievement_system.d: A persistent milestone system that records notable actions, grants recognition, and may unlock rewards.
e: An achievement is added after players already satisfied its requirement and needs retroactive unlock logic.
A tracked_event_id fires multiple times during replay, reconnect, or save migration.
Secret achievements need progress tracking without revealing hidden text prematurely.
b: Achievement completion is stored locally but the reward_grant_id runs every login.
Progress counters reset during save migration because achievement_id changed.
UI listens to predicted events and shows completion for actions later rejected by the server.
t: Achievement rewards should not force every player into obscure challenge behavior unless they are optional cosmetics or small bonuses.
Use a mix of short, medium, and long thresholds so the system has visible progress without becoming checklist noise.
a: Provide text descriptions, progress counters, and a way to review missed notifications.
Avoid requiring precision-only or sensory-only challenges for mandatory progression rewards without alternate routes.

progression.crafting_unlocks.d: A progression rule that makes recipes, stations, material tiers, or crafting categories available over time.
e: A recipe is unlocked but the required station tier is missing or destroyed.
A patch moves a recipe to a new unlock_requirement_id while old saves already know it.
Multiplayer crafting stations need to decide whether unlocks belong to the account, character, party, or world.
b: Crafting UI checks recipe visibility while the transaction validator checks a different unlock table.
Blueprint pickups grant duplicate recipes because recipe_id completion is not idempotent.
Retroactive unlock scans run every login and repeatedly display the same recipe notifications.
t: Unlock recipe groups in clusters that create new choices, not just one strictly superior replacement at a time.
Late recipes should account for material drop rates and station costs so unlocking does not immediately bottleneck elsewhere.
a: Show locked recipes with readable requirement text when spoilers are acceptable.
Provide sorting and filtering by station, material tier, and unlock source for large recipe lists.

progression.equipment_rarity.d: A tiering system that groups equipment by scarcity, power budget, presentation, and upgrade potential.
p: rarity_tier: common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary
e: A low-level high-rarity item can be weaker than a later common item and confuse players if comparison is unclear.
Rarity tiers added in a patch need migration for old items and loot tables.
Duplicate unique items require a rule for ownership, conversion, or rerolling.
b: Rarity color updates but stat_budget_multiplier does not, producing misleading items.
Loot tables filter by display rarity name instead of rarity_tier, breaking localization and balance tools.
Upgrade caps are checked in UI but not in the upgrade transaction.
t: Rarity should change expected value, not guarantee that every item invalidates lower tiers immediately.
The rarest tier needs enough drop scarcity and upgrade cost to stay exciting without making ordinary rewards worthless.
a: Communicate rarity with text labels and icons in addition to color.
Make item comparison readable with explicit stat changes, not only rarity names or glow effects.

progression.experience_points.d: A numeric progression resource earned from play and accumulated toward levels, unlocks, or reward thresholds.
e: One reward crosses multiple level_threshold_table entries and must grant every level reward exactly once.
XP is awarded while the player is at cap and later the cap increases.
A quest reward is retried after disconnect and must not duplicate xp_source_id grants.
b: The UI increments XP optimistically but save data only stores the old value after a crash.
Multiple-level gains grant only the first skill point or unlock because the loop stops after one threshold.
XP is stored as a floating point value and threshold comparisons fail near exact boundaries.
t: Tune XP sources against expected session length and desired unlock cadence, not only enemy difficulty.
Large one-time rewards need overflow handling so they do not waste player effort at caps.
a: Show current XP, next threshold, and reward preview in readable text.
Avoid progress bars with no numeric context for players who need precise planning information.

progression.level_up.d: A threshold-crossing event that increases a player, character, account, or system level and grants associated rewards.
e: A single XP grant crosses several levels and must apply every stat and reward in order.
A max level cap increases after players stored overflow XP or reached the old cap.
Level rewards change in a patch and existing saves need retroactive_reward_policy handling.
b: Only one level reward is granted during multi-level gains.
Derived stats recalculate before equipment or skill modifiers are reloaded, causing temporary wrong values.
Level-up notifications play before persistence, so a crash loses the reward but not the memory of seeing it.
t: Early levels should arrive quickly enough to teach the loop; later thresholds can stretch only if rewards stay desirable.
Large power jumps need content difficulty, gear, and enemy scaling to account for the new level state.
a: Provide a reviewable summary of level rewards after the animation finishes.
Do not rely only on flashing effects or loud audio to communicate a level-up.

progression.meta_progression.d: Progress that persists beyond a single run, match, character life, or session and changes future attempts.
e: A run ends during a crash or disconnect and must decide which rewards leave run_progression_state.
A permanent unlock is removed or rebalanced in a patch and needs compensation or migration.
Players share a device but need separate account_progression_state records.
b: Run-only buffs leak into account_progression_state and become permanent.
Meta currency is granted on both run end and result screen reopen because reward transaction IDs are not stored.
Save migration resets permanent_unlock_flag values when unlock definitions move.
t: Meta progression should reduce frustration without making player skill irrelevant.
Permanent power needs caps, branching choices, or escalating costs to avoid flattening the difficulty curve.
a: Make the difference between temporary run rewards and permanent account rewards explicit in UI text.
Offer progress summaries after a run so players can review gains at their own pace.

progression.prestige_reset.d: A reset that trades current progression for a permanent reward, multiplier, unlock, or new progression layer.
e: A player triggers prestige while pending rewards, purchases, or crafting transactions are unresolved.
Reset scope includes abilities used to access the current area, risking a soft-lock after prestige.
Repeated prestige bonuses hit cap and need a clear explanation of remaining value.
b: Reset clears the reward currency before prestige_reward_id is granted.
Temporary run bonuses are accidentally copied into permanent account_progression_state.
Confirmation preview omits items, currencies, or unlocks that will be lost.
t: Prestige rewards should make the next loop feel different, not only numerically faster.
Reset cost must respect player time investment; irreversible resets need unusually clear previews.
a: Require clear confirmation with a checklist of lost and retained progress.
Allow players to review prestige benefits and reset consequences without a countdown or pressure timer.

progression.respec.d: A system that lets players refund and reassign progression choices without rebuilding the entire save or character from scratch.
e: Refunding a prerequisite must remove, disable, or block dependent abilities before the build can be saved.
Removed abilities need cleanup for hotbars, passives, summons, equipment requirements, and active cooldowns.
Balance patches may need free respec grants or forced rebuilds for invalid node IDs.
b: Passive stat bonuses remain after the node is refunded because derived stats are patched instead of rebuilt.
UI shows refunded points before validation and loses them on save reload.
Respec allows invalid builds that cannot be reloaded later because prerequisite graph validation is skipped.
t: Cheap respec supports experimentation; expensive respec reinforces identity and long-term planning.
Punishing respec costs can discourage players from engaging with complex trees.
a: Provide confirmation, preview, and undo steps so players do not lose progress through accidental clicks.

progression.skill_tree.d: A graph or branching structure where players spend progression resources to unlock abilities, passives, or build modifiers.
e: Removing a prerequisite node during respec must also remove or disable dependent nodes.
Content patches that move or rename node_id values need migration rules for existing saves.
UI navigation must handle large trees with keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touch, zoom, and search.
b: A node can be purchased without prerequisites because UI and backend validation differ.
Refunding a node leaves granted abilities, passive stats, or hotbar actions active.
Circular prerequisites lock the tree or make validation recurse forever.
t: Avoid mandatory tax nodes that every build must buy unless they serve a clear tutorial purpose.
Powerful synergies need opportunity cost, branch distance, class restriction, or diminishing returns.
a: Support zoom, search, readable focus order, and text scaling for large trees.
Use icons plus text labels so node meaning is not carried only by color or shape.

progression.unlockable_abilities.d: A progression rule that grants new verbs, powers, passives, or interaction options after requirements are met.
e: An ability unlocks while the player is airborne, in combat, or in a menu and should not steal input unexpectedly.
A removed prerequisite must decide whether to keep, refund, or revoke already granted abilities.
Abilities used for traversal can soft-lock saves if revoked while the player is behind a gate.
b: Ability UI appears unlocked but the input binding or action map is not enabled.
Save data stores display names instead of ability_id, breaking migration and localization.
Retroactive unlocks grant the same ability multiple times because grant transaction IDs are not tracked.
t: New verbs should arrive when the game has space to teach and test them, not only when the XP curve needs a reward.
Traversal abilities can invalidate old level layouts, so gating and backtracking should be planned together.
a: Provide input remapping and tutorial review for newly unlocked actions.
Avoid locking required accessibility assists behind progression; capability unlocks should not gate basic playability.

progression.upgrade_shop.d: A shop-like progression interface where players spend currency or materials to improve stats, abilities, equipment, or account perks.
e: A player can afford an upgrade when the panel opens but spends the resource elsewhere before confirmation.
An upgrade changes a stat that affects current health, stamina, inventory capacity, or active cooldowns.
Prerequisite upgrades are refunded or removed after dependent upgrades have already been purchased.
b: Wallet is debited but upgrade_effect_payload_id fails to apply, leaving the save in a half-purchased state.
Purchase buttons check prerequisites in UI but the commit path accepts invalid prerequisite_upgrade_ids.
Stackable upgrades exceed purchase_limit after save/load because count is stored in UI state.
t: Upgrade costs should be tuned against actual currency and material source rates, not only desired tier order.
Permanent upgrades need escalating costs, prerequisites, or caps to avoid flattening challenge too early.
a: Show current level, next effect, full cost, missing resources, and purchase limit in one readable view.
Provide confirmation or undo for expensive upgrades that permanently change a build.

puzzle.color_matching.d: The player aligns colored channels, symbols, lights, or objects so the current pattern matches the required solution.
p: color_channel_id: red, blue, green, amber, symbol_triangle
channel_assignment_map: slot ids mapped to channel ids
solution_state_hash: hash of canonical channel assignment
e: Two colors are visually similar under lighting, post-processing, or colorblind display modes.
A channel changes during animation while validation reads the previous assignment.
The puzzle is solved by symbols but the UI still reports only color names.
b: Validation compares display color values instead of stable color_channel_id identifiers.
Hint state reveals an old solution after designers reorder channels in content data.
A solved state fires repeatedly when players continue rotating already-correct pieces.
t: A good color puzzle should be solvable from structure, symbols, or placement, not color alone.
More channels increase difficulty quickly; use grouping or intermediate feedback for larger sets.
a: Always pair color with icons, labels, shapes, patterns, or placement cues.
Offer high-contrast and colorblind-safe palettes for puzzle-critical channels.

puzzle.key_and_lock.d: A lock blocks progress until the player presents, consumes, or proves ownership of a required key item.
e: The player unlocks a door and reloads before the key removal and lock state are both persisted.
Two players try to unlock the same shared lock with different keys in the same server tick.
A key is optional for one route but required to avoid a later soft-lock.
b: The key is consumed but the lock remains closed after an interrupted animation or scene transition.
Unlock prompts appear for players who lack the key because UI checks a stale inventory snapshot.
Duplicate interaction events consume multiple stack units for one lock.
t: Required keys should be placed where players can infer the route back to the lock.
