Reusable keys reduce inventory friction but can weaken the sense of one-time progression.
a: Show the required key name or icon in text form, and make missing-key messages persistent enough to read.
Consider map or journal reminders for locks the player has found but cannot yet open.

puzzle.lever_switch.d: An interactable switch changes state and drives linked targets such as doors, platforms, hazards, or logic nodes.
p: switch_state: off, on, locked, returning, disabled
e: A switch is pulled while linked door animation is still moving from the previous state.
Multiple switches control one target and their dependency graph reaches a contradictory state.
A player saves after the switch changed but before all target events finished.
b: Lever animation changes locally but linked target state is rejected by authority validation.
Switch state resets visually after load while the door remains open.
Events fire in nondeterministic order and multi-switch puzzles become unsolvable after repeated toggles.
t: Players should be able to see, hear, or infer at least one linked target when learning a new switch rule.
Timed return switches should give enough margin for route reading, not only perfect execution.
a: Use persistent visual position, text prompts, and audio cues to show switch state.
Avoid making critical switches distinguishable only by small red/green light changes.

puzzle.mirror_light_reflection.d: Players rotate or place reflectors so a simulated light path reaches receivers, filters, or targets.
e: A mirror rotates while the raycast update is evaluating later bounces.
Two mirrors create a loop that repeatedly hits the same reflectors.
A moving blocker interrupts a beam after the receiver has already opened a door.
b: Floating-point drift makes a visually aligned mirror miss the receiver by a tiny angle.
Raycasts hit the mirror's back face or decorative mesh instead of the intended reflective plane.
Receivers remain active after the ray is blocked because deactivation events are not emitted.
t: Snap increments make optical puzzles easier to reason about than free rotation.
Long bounce chains should expose intermediate beam segments so players can locate the mistake.
a: Use beam thickness, receiver labels, sound, and icons in addition to color.
Offer reduced glare and high-contrast beam rendering for players sensitive to bright effects.

puzzle.physics_weight_puzzle.d: Players use object mass, placement, buoyancy, gravity, or balance to satisfy a physical puzzle condition.
e: A required object falls into an unreachable pit or is destroyed by another system.
Physics sleep makes an object appear stable while tiny motion still changes the solved state.
Two lighter objects stack in a way the designer did not intend but still pass the mass threshold.
b: Every collider on one object contributes mass separately and over-activates the puzzle.
Object reset runs while the player is carrying the object and teleports it away.
Solvability tools ignore locked doors or one-way ledges that block object return routes.
t: Object classes should visually communicate relative weight so solutions feel deduced, not guessed.
Physics tolerance is important; near-solved arrangements should not flicker rapidly.
a: Provide readable target zones and optional hints for which object classes can contribute.
Avoid requiring precise analog object placement without snap, guide, or reset support.

puzzle.portal_pair.d: Two linked surfaces or volumes remap position, velocity, orientation, visibility, or objects across space.
e: An object is partially inside the portal and collides with both rooms during the same step.
Two portals face each other and create an infinite transfer loop.
The exit portal moves, rotates, or becomes blocked while a body is crossing.
b: Velocity is mapped but angular velocity, camera pitch, or carried objects are not.
Teleport lockout is global and prevents other actors from using the portal pair.
Collision correction pushes the player back into the entry portal and causes flicker.
t: Portals are easier to reason about when entry and exit surfaces have strong visual identity.
Momentum-preserving portals create expressive solutions but require larger safety margins around exits.
a: Offer comfort options for sudden camera rotation, FOV shifts, and rapid visual recursion.
Use labels, colors plus shapes, or directional arrows so linked endpoints are identifiable.

puzzle.pressure_plate.d: A floor trigger activates when enough valid bodies or objects rest inside its tracked volume.
e: Two objects enter and one exits during the same physics tick, changing threshold ordering.
A stacked object rests on another object that rests on the plate and should or should not count.
A carried object is inside the trigger volume but not actually resting on the plate surface.
b: Trigger exit is missed when a physics body is destroyed, pooled, or teleported away.
Every overlapping collider on one object contributes mass and activates the plate incorrectly.
Release delay fires after the plate reactivated, closing a door on the player.
t: Plate surfaces should be large enough for intended objects but not so large that accidental activation is common.
Weighted plates are easier to read when object mass classes are visually distinct.
a: Use plate depression, sound, light, and linked-target indicators so activation is not conveyed only by color.
Avoid requiring extremely precise object placement unless the level supports camera and input assists.

puzzle.sequence_memory.d: The player observes or discovers an ordered sequence, then repeats it through buttons, symbols, notes, or interactions.
p: activation_order: red, blue, green or button ids
e: A player presses two inputs during the same frame or network tick.
The sequence clue is visible only once and the player reloads after seeing half of it.
Wrong input should reset the step index but not reset other solved room state.
b: The displayed replay sequence differs from activation_order after localization or content edits.
Step index is saved after input but before the success event, causing repeated final-step rewards.
Audio-only cues fail for players with muted sound because no alternate clue path exists.
t: Longer sequences should be paired with stronger clue repetition or chunking.
Wrong-input penalties should match the puzzle tone; harsh resets are poor fits for long memory chains.
a: Provide non-audio alternatives for sound sequences and non-color alternatives for color sequences.
Offer replay, notes, slower presentation, or hint-stage options for players with memory or perception differences.

puzzle.sliding_block.d: Players move blocks across constrained spaces to cover targets, open routes, or reach a solved arrangement.
p: move_lock_state: idle, moving, blocked, falling, locked
e: A block is pushed into a corner where no legal move can recover it.
The player saves after a block starts moving but before it reaches the next grid cell.
Two blocks are pushed into the same destination cell by simultaneous interactions.
b: Block visuals move smoothly but grid_cell_coordinate updates early, allowing invalid overlapping moves.
Undo restores position but not linked pressure plate or door state.
Reset returns blocks to anchors while the player is standing in the destination cell.
t: Small block puzzles benefit from undo; larger puzzles need reset shortcuts and readable goals.
Irreversible moves can create tension but should be used sparingly unless reset is fast.
a: Provide undo or reset options for long spatial puzzles to reduce repetitive recovery.
Use high-contrast target markers and grid alignment cues so block goals are readable.

puzzle.timed_door.d: A door or gate opens after a trigger and closes again when a countdown, condition, or reset rule expires.
e: The player crosses the door threshold on the same tick that the close window expires.
The start trigger is pressed again while the door is opening, open, closing, or blocked.
A save occurs with the door open and only part of the countdown remaining.
b: Door visuals close but collision remains open, or collision closes before animation communicates it.
Countdown UI rounds differently from authority state and shows one second remaining after closure.
Pause menu freezes the animation but not the underlying timer.
t: Timed doors should test route planning more than loading screens, camera confusion, or animation delay.
Grace windows and checkpoint placement reduce frustration without removing urgency.
a: Show countdown state with text, audio cues, animation, and icon changes rather than sound alone.
Offer relaxed timers or alternate routes where strict execution is not the main challenge.

rhythm.beat_matching.d: A mechanic where player inputs are evaluated against musical beat positions using an audio clock, chart data, and latency-adjusted judgment windows.
p: song_id: track or music cue id
e: The audio device reports a playhead jump after pause, buffering, or output-device change.
A player input arrives between two valid beats and could be consumed by either note.
The game drops render frames while audio playback continues correctly.
b: Input is judged against frame delta instead of audio_playhead_ms, causing drift under load.
Latency offset is applied twice to held notes or repeated taps.
Pause resumes chart scrolling but not the audio clock baseline.
t: Tighter windows increase mastery but magnify device latency and accessibility barriers.
Early and late feedback should be symmetrical unless the music or control scheme has a deliberate bias.
a: Provide audio latency calibration, visual latency calibration, and per-player offset profiles.
Offer wider timing windows or practice modes for players with motor or device-latency constraints.

rhythm.combo_multiplier.d: A scoring layer that increases rewards for consecutive successful rhythm judgments and resets or reduces value when misses, breaks, or invalid inputs occur.
p: multiplier_tier_id: x1, x2, x4, x8, overdrive
e: A simultaneous chord has one perfect note and one missed lane input.
A hold note starts successfully but releases early during an otherwise valid streak.
A pause or disconnect occurs after a hit but before combo feedback displays.
b: Combo increments per visual effect instead of per committed hit_judgment_id.
Misses break combo twice for one note because both miss cleanup and input failure emit events.
Multiplier tier updates after score calculation, applying the old tier to the wrong note.
t: High multipliers make full-combo play exciting but can make early mistakes feel unrecoverable.
Grace systems are useful for accessibility and casual modes when they are surfaced honestly in scoring.
a: Allow reduced visual clutter for combo effects while keeping essential streak state visible.
Offer assist profiles that soften combo breaks without hiding the scoring difference.

rhythm.note_lane.d: A visual and logical lane that maps charted notes to specific input channels, spawn positions, scroll behavior, and hit targets.
p: note_id: unique note or hold-note identifier
e: Two notes in the same lane overlap visually but need separate input windows.
A scroll-rate change occurs while notes are already visible.
A hold note crosses a pause boundary or tempo-map transition.
b: Rendered note position drifts from audio-clock judgment because animation uses frame delta.
Lane input mapping changes in settings but existing spawned notes keep old lane ids.
Miss cleanup removes notes visually before the judgment system records the miss.
t: More lanes increase reading difficulty even if note density stays the same.
Scroll profiles should preserve anticipation; very fast lanes need strong calibration and practice support.
a: Provide high-contrast, colorblind-safe, enlarged-target, and reduced-clutter lane profiles.
Allow players to remap lane inputs and preview lane layout before songs.

rhythm.sync_window.d: A set of latency-adjusted judgment bands that classify inputs as perfect, good, late, early, missed, or ignored relative to charted beat timestamps.
p: hit_judgment_id: perfect, good, early, late, miss
e: Two notes are close enough that one input could fall inside both judgment windows.
A held note begins with a perfect hit but releases outside the allowed end band.
Calibration changes while a note is active and should apply only after the current chart segment.
b: Judgment windows are checked in a non-deterministic note order and consume inputs inconsistently.
Miss cleanup uses render position instead of audio-clock position.
Early and late offsets are displayed with reversed signs.
t: Window sizes should match song density, input device, and intended rank difficulty.
Perfect windows can be strict if good windows preserve playability and feedback is accurate.
a: Offer adjustable timing windows or assist profiles separate from audiovisual latency calibration.
Show early and late feedback in text or clear symbols, not only color.

roguelike.curse_modifier.d: A harmful or complicating run modifier that changes rules, rewards, enemies, resources, or player options until removed or the run ends.
e: A curse removes the only action, resource, or item needed to complete the current floor.
Two curses modify the same reward_pool_id and produce impossible or empty reward choices.
A curse is accepted in a shop or event and then the run is saved before UI state closes.
b: Stacking curses multiply each other because modifiers are applied repeatedly during stat recompute.
Hidden curses trigger without any readable cause and feel like a random bug to the player.
Removal clears the visual icon but leaves the gameplay modifier in the run_state_snapshot.
t: A curse paired with a reward should change play style, not simply tax the player after the reward is already taken.
Stacking rules need caps or compatibility tags so curses do not combine into unwinnable states.
a: Show curse effects in plain language with persistent access from the run HUD or pause screen.
Use icon, text, and audio cues for curse activation rather than color alone.

roguelike.permadeath.d: A run failure rule where character defeat or another terminal condition ends the current run and discards most run-scoped progress.
p: run_state_snapshot: health, inventory, floor, modifiers, seed cursor
e: The player disconnects or crashes after lethal damage but before post-run rewards are committed.
A revive, invulnerability frame, or delayed damage tick arrives during the death resolution sequence.
Victory and death conditions happen during the same simulation step.
b: Run-scoped inventory leaks into account state because cleanup runs after reward grants.
Post-run rewards are granted twice when death resolution retries after a network timeout.
The game saves a fatal checkpoint and reloads into an unavoidable death loop.
t: Permanent run loss is easier to accept when runs are short enough or post-run learning is obvious.
Meta rewards can soften failure, but too much account power can make early-run decisions irrelevant.
a: Provide confirmation and readable consequences for abandoning or deleting a run.
Offer practice, assist, or non-competitive modes if the full run-loss rule blocks players from learning.

roguelike.pick_one_upgrade_choice.d: A run reward screen where the player chooses one upgrade from a small generated set and commits it to the current build.
p: reward_choice_id: unique per offered reward screen
e: All generated options become invalid after another system changes inventory or build tags.
A reroll uses the same reward_choice_id and redraws identical options from the same RNG cursor.
Two options are technically different but share the same visible effect and feel duplicated.
b: Selection commits on button down and again on confirm, granting two upgrades.
Preview text uses post-selection state and shows inflated synergy effects.
Reroll price is charged even if reward generation fails and falls back to the old set.
t: Too much synergy bias makes runs solve themselves; too little makes builds feel disconnected.
Choice slot count changes both decision difficulty and average build power.
a: Show full option text, comparison hints, and keyword explanations without requiring fast reading.
Support controller, keyboard, and screen-reader ordering that matches the visual option order.

roguelike.procedural_floor.d: A run-scoped floor generator that combines topology, placed rooms, encounters, rewards, shops, bosses, exits, difficulty pacing, and persistence for the current roguelike run.
e: A locked room appears before the key or traversal ability needed to reach its reward.
The only exit is generated behind an encounter that can despawn or become unreachable.
A shop, rest room, or boss node occupies a layout socket too small for required actors.
b: Layout RNG and reward RNG share a stream, so adding a decoration changes combat rewards.
Validation checks connectivity but not collision, navmesh, or camera framing inside room templates.
Room graph ids are regenerated on load, breaking map reveal and visited-room persistence.
t: Longer critical paths increase commitment and resource attrition; optional branches should compensate with meaningful rewards or information.
Too many safe rooms, shops, or recovery nodes can flatten tension even when combat rooms are difficult.
a: Provide map readability for generated layouts, including visited state, exits, and branch types.
Avoid requiring players to memorize long procedural routes without landmarks or map support.

roguelike.random_powerups.d: A generated reward mechanic that grants run-scoped powerups from weighted pools after rooms, events, shops, bosses, or pickups.
e: The reward pool is empty after unlock filters, duplicate rules, and character restrictions apply.
A granted powerup changes eligibility for other options in the same reward screen.
A save reload happens after the drop appears but before the player collects it.
b: Reward draws are not deterministic because pool iteration follows unordered dictionary keys.
Duplicate prevention checks display names instead of stable powerup ids.
Temporary powerups persist after floor transition because cleanup does not inspect powerup_instance_id.
t: Reward weighting should support both build discovery and comeback potential without guaranteeing ideal synergies.
Permanent unlocks increase pool size, so older content may need weighting or tags to stay visible.
a: Provide clear text for powerup effects, stack behavior, and whether the effect is temporary.
Let players review collected powerups outside fast reward moments.

roguelike.relic_synergy.d: An interaction pattern where two or more run items, relics, cards, or modifiers produce stronger, altered, or newly enabled behavior together.
p: debug_reason_trace: effect id and contributing relic ids
e: Two relics trigger each other recursively and create an infinite event loop.
A relic is removed or transformed while another relic is iterating over active instances.
Synergy tags change after an upgrade and invalidate cached tooltip text.
b: Effect order follows collection order and changes after save/load sorting.
Stack caps apply per relic definition instead of per relic_instance_id, breaking duplicate behavior.
Tooltips advertise a synergy from tags that are not eligible in the current room or mode.
t: Strong synergies are memorable, but every build archetype needs enough counterweights and dead-end prevention.
Explicit pair synergies are easier to tune; tag-based synergies scale better but need caps and telemetry.
a: Expose synergy previews and active combo explanations in tooltips or a run log.
Avoid relying on players remembering item names from earlier rooms; show current contributing relics.

roguelike.risk_reward_room.d: An optional room or encounter that offers stronger rewards in exchange for extra danger, resource loss, curses, elite enemies, or route commitment.
e: The player accepts the risk, leaves the room, and reloads before completion or failure is resolved.
Reward pickup becomes reachable before the encounter actually clears.
A curse or payment is applied, but the room generation fails and no encounter starts.
b: Room state resets on reload and lets players retry the risk after seeing the encounter.
Rewards are generated from a fresh seed after completion and differ from the preview or replay.
Exit doors unlock from enemy despawn instead of authoritative encounter clear state.
t: The best risk rooms offer a real refusal path; mandatory risk feels like baseline difficulty rather than a choice.
Rewards should match the danger type: resource payment can grant build power, while combat risk can grant rare items or route advantage.
a: Make the accepted risk readable in text before the player commits.
Provide enough contrast, audio alternatives, and map labels for optional high-danger rooms.

roguelike.run_based_progression.d: A progression structure where power, resources, map state, and build choices accumulate inside a single run and reset or convert when the run ends.
p: run_state_snapshot: build, resources, map, modifiers, rng cursors
run_event_log_id: stable log id for ordered run events
e: The player earns a permanent unlock while holding temporary run items with similar ids.
A save migrates after reward definitions change but before the run reaches its summary screen.
A reconnect restores account state but not the current run_state_snapshot.
b: Temporary run currency is saved in the same wallet as account currency.
Unlocks are granted when a reward is previewed instead of when it is committed.
Difficulty scaling reads total account progress and unintentionally punishes experienced players in fresh runs.
t: Strong run growth is satisfying when early weakness remains short and readable.
Meta progression should widen future possibilities more than it invalidates current-run skill.
a: Let players review current run build, modifiers, and recent decisions in a readable summary.
Avoid hiding critical progression state inside tiny icons or transient notifications.

roguelike.shop_between_levels.d: A shop or rest stop placed between floors where players spend run currency on items, healing, removals, upgrades, rerolls, or information.
p: shop_inventory_seed: derived from run_seed and floor_index
e: The player saves in a shop after buying an item but before the next floor is generated.
A reroll replaces an item that the player has selected but not confirmed.
A shop offer becomes invalid because an account unlock or curse changes eligible pools.
b: Shop inventory regenerates on reload and lets players fish for better offers.
Sold-out state is stored visually but not in run data, so the item returns after reopening.
Reroll pricing reads account currency instead of run_currency_id.
t: Shop prices should reflect the opportunity cost between healing, build power, and future flexibility.
Guaranteed shops reduce frustration, but too many can make floor rewards less exciting.
a: Provide clear comparison text for current resources, purchase results, and sold-out state.
Require confirmable purchase actions for expensive or irreversible offers.

simulation.needs_simulation.d: A tick-based model where agents or player characters track needs such as hunger, rest, morale, hygiene, comfort, or safety and react to thresholds.
p: need_state_id: hunger, rest, morale, warmth, hygiene
recovery_source_id: meal, bed, shelter, medicine, entertainment
e: An agent is asleep, injured, traveling, or in storage while needs continue to update.
A recovery source is consumed but the target need state changed before the transaction commits.
Offline progress would kill or permanently disable agents before the player can react.
b: Needs update in render frames instead of simulation ticks and vary by frame rate.
Threshold effects fire repeatedly because the previous band is not stored.
Recovery consumes inventory client-side before the simulation accepts the state change.
t: Need decay should create planning pressure before it creates unavoidable failure.
More need categories increase systemic depth but also increase UI and cognitive load.
a: Provide readable need labels, threshold warnings, and sortable agent lists.
Avoid requiring players to infer urgent needs from tiny icons alone.

simulation.population_model.d: A world-state model that tracks groups of agents, citizens, creatures, or factions through spawning, migration, growth, attrition, demand, and capacity rules.
p: demand_curve_id: jobs, food, shelter, territory, safety
e: A region loses capacity after a disaster and must decide which agents migrate or despawn.
Visible agents and aggregate population counts diverge after pooling or save/load.
Population growth runs offline and exceeds food, shelter, or performance budgets.
b: Spawned agents are counted again as population growth when folded back into aggregate state.
Despawn pooling removes quest-critical or player-targeted entities.
Population ticks use unordered region maps and produce non-reproducible results.
t: Aggregate populations let designers simulate scale, but players need enough visible agents to believe the model.
Hard capacity caps are readable; soft caps can feel more organic but need explanation.
a: Provide readable dashboards, map overlays, and alert thresholds for population changes.
Avoid relying on dense crowd visuals alone to communicate population state.

simulation.systemic_weather.d: A world-state weather system where conditions transition over simulation time and affect visibility, movement, resources, AI, audio, or survival pressure.
p: weather_state_id: clear, rain, storm, snow, heatwave, fog
e: The player saves during a transition between weather states.
Weather affects visibility but accessibility settings increase scene brightness.
A biome transition crosses two incompatible weather profiles.
b: Visual rain starts before gameplay wet-road or exposure modifiers are active.
Weather transition RNG is not saved and changes after reload.
Forecast UI reads planned state while gameplay uses current weather_state_id.
t: Weather penalties should be telegraphed before they invalidate plans or routes.
Frequent transitions make the world lively but can obscure player cause and effect.
a: Provide reduced storm flash, reduced wind noise, and visibility assist settings.
Keep critical UI and subtitles readable during fog, rain, snow, or darkness effects.

simulation.traffic_flow.d: A network simulation where vehicles, agents, or abstract traffic units choose routes, occupy lanes, respond to signals, and create congestion or throughput effects.
e: A route becomes invalid after the player deletes a road or changes direction rules.
Visible vehicles reach a blocked intersection while aggregate flow still assumes capacity.
An emergency or scripted vehicle needs priority without corrupting normal traffic order.
b: Vehicle agents choose paths before updated road ownership or lane closures are committed.
Despawning offscreen vehicles loses passengers, cargo, or delivery state.
Traffic signals update after vehicles move and allow impossible intersection overlaps.
t: Traffic should expose bottlenecks early enough for players to diagnose them.
Fully realistic traffic can be less playable than a model with clear capacity and routing rules.
a: Provide colorblind-safe congestion overlays with numeric or patterned alternatives.
Let players slow or pause the simulation while inspecting complex intersections.

stealth.alert_state.d: An AI perception state machine that moves agents between unaware, suspicious, searching, alerted, and combat-ready behavior based on perception events.
e: A guard hears a noise and sees the player in the same decision tick, requiring deterministic perception priority.
The player breaks line of sight during the grace interval and leaves a last_known_player_position for search.
Checkpoint restore should not resurrect a combat alert unless that state was intentionally saved.
b: Suspicion oscillates every tick because threshold and decay have no hysteresis margin.
AI enters combat without storing the perception_event_id that caused the transition.
Awareness UI shows suspicious while behavior tree already selected attack actions.
t: Long grace windows make stealth more forgiving; short windows favor strict line-of-sight play.
Group alert propagation can make a single mistake cascade, so squads need distance or communication limits.
a: Represent alert state with shape, text, or meter changes in addition to color.
Provide non-audio cues for suspicion gain caused by sound events so deaf or low-volume players can read the system.

stealth.distraction_throw.d: A thrown or placed object that creates a perception event, drawing AI investigation toward a target position without directly revealing the player.
e: A distraction lands outside the navmesh and needs a reachable investigation_target_position.
An AI sees the thrown object or throw arc and should react differently from hearing only the impact.
Multiple distractions in one squad need deterministic priority and cooldown rules.
b: AI paths to the raw impact point even when it is unreachable or inside collision.
Noise radius ignores doors, floors, and sound occlusion policy, attracting enemies through entire buildings.
The object keeps emitting lure events after pickup, despawn, or checkpoint reload.
t: Cheap reusable distractions can solve every patrol unless AI learns, cools down, or verifies false alarms.
High priority lure events are powerful because they override patrol, search, and sometimes combat tasks.
a: Show a preview or after-impact cue for lure radius when the game expects precise sound placement.
Provide non-audio confirmation that the distraction was heard and which guards are investigating.

stealth.last_known_position_search.d: An AI search behavior that stores the player location from the latest credible perception event and investigates it after direct detection is lost.
e: The last known point is inside a locked room, off navmesh, or behind a door the AI cannot open.
A newer noise event and older visual sighting compete for the same AI search slot.
Checkpoint restore during search needs to restore or intentionally clear search state consistently.
b: AI updates last_known_player_position every frame through walls because line-of-sight grace never expires.
Search path fails when the remembered point is unreachable and the behavior tree has no fallback.
False clues overwrite confirmed visual contact without priority comparison.
t: Long stale intervals make AI feel persistent; short intervals make stealth recovery easier.
Search radius should match level room size and cover density so investigation feels believable.
a: Provide readable non-audio indicators when enemies begin searching the last known position.
Avoid hidden omniscience; players should see or infer why a search moved to a specific area.

stealth.noise_meter.d: A player- or AI-facing model of how much sound the player generates, how far it propagates, and which agents can hear it.
e: A loud action in another room should account for sound_occlusion_policy_id instead of alerting every nearby AI equally.
Stacked actions such as sprinting while reloading need a rule for combining or prioritizing noise events.
Moving platforms and vehicles may contribute their own noise source separate from player footsteps.
b: Noise UI displays raw loudness while AI uses occluded loudness, making player feedback misleading.
Surface material lookup samples the wrong foot position and changes loudness every step unpredictably.
Crouch noise multiplier stacks repeatedly after stance transitions.
t: High surface contrast makes route choice meaningful; low contrast turns noise into a decorative meter.
Hearing thresholds should be tuned with patrol spacing and ambient audio cover, not only action loudness.
a: Provide visual noise indicators and subtitles or icons for sound-based AI reactions.
Avoid relying only on stereo audio direction when noise placement is part of stealth problem solving.

stealth.shadow_cover.d: A stealth modifier where darkness, cover volumes, and light sampling reduce how easily AI vision systems detect the player.
p: shadow_cover_id: volume id or sampled zone id
e: Dynamic lights can move over the player while AI vision is between decision ticks.
Camera auto-exposure may make an area look dark to the player while AI light sampling reads it as bright.
Particles, muzzle flashes, or flashlights need rules for temporary visibility spikes.
b: Light sampling reads only one foot point and misses the upper body in bright light.
Shadow cover volume remains active after a door opens or object moves away.
AI and UI use different visibility curves and disagree about whether the player is hidden.
t: Strong shadow protection supports classic stealth but can trivialize AI unless patrol routes include light pressure.
Graded visibility gives designers more tuning room than binary hidden/exposed states.
a: Use UI state, outline strength, or icons in addition to subtle brightness differences.
Avoid requiring players to distinguish very dark tones without contrast, gamma, or visibility assists.

stealth.visibility_meter.d: A player-facing and AI-facing measure of how detectable the character is based on light, stance, movement, distance, cover, and enemy perception rules.
e: Different enemies may see the player from different distances or angles while one global meter is shown.
The player can be hidden from sight but loud enough to trigger hearing, requiring separate noise messaging.
Camera occlusion can make the player feel covered even when AI vision rays have a clear line.
b: The UI meter uses player camera exposure while AI uses world light samples.
Movement visibility multiplier remains applied after sprinting stops.
Cover volumes overlap and multiply into near-zero visibility when only the strongest modifier was intended.
t: Precise meters support fair stealth but can reduce uncertainty; vague meters preserve tension but need strong feedback on failure.
Visibility scoring must be tuned with level lighting and patrol sightlines, not only character stance.
a: Use text, icons, or shape changes alongside color to represent hidden, watched, and detected states.
Allow meter size and contrast adjustments because stealth relies heavily on reading this signal.

strategy.fog_of_war.d: A map information system where terrain, units, resources, or enemy actions are hidden until revealed by scouts, sensors, ownership, or shared team vision.
p: player_id: local player or commander id
e: A unit dies or transfers ownership during the same tick it reveals enemy units.
Team alliances change and shared vision must update without leaking old enemy intel.
A replay or spectator view needs broader visibility than the active player had.
b: Minimap fog and world fog use different cell grids and show conflicting information.
Hidden enemy units are sent to clients and can be exposed by modded UI or memory inspection.
Visibility updates after combat resolution, allowing attacks from unrevealed targets.
t: Scout radius, terrain blockers, and unit mobility define how expensive information is.
Team-shared vision can reduce coordination friction but may weaken scouting roles.
a: Use texture, opacity, labels, or outlines in addition to color to distinguish fog states.
Keep minimap and main-map fog language consistent for players with low vision.

strategy.tech_tree.d: A structured research or unlock graph where players spend resources, meet prerequisites, and unlock units, buildings, upgrades, policies, or strategic options.
p: prerequisite_node_ids: zero or more tech ids
e: A technology is removed or renamed in an update while a save has it queued.
Two prerequisite branches complete on the same tick and unlock a dependent node.
A player loses the building or territory required to continue active research.
b: Unlock effects apply when research starts instead of when it completes.
Research queue UI accepts a node but server validation rejects missing prerequisites.
Progress is stored by display name and breaks after localization or balance updates.
t: Early tech choices should open options quickly; late tech choices can carry heavier commitment.
Mutually exclusive branches need enough information for players to understand what they are giving up.
a: Provide searchable tree views, prerequisite explanations, and clear blocked-state reasons.
Avoid communicating branch types only through color or tiny icons.

strategy.territory_control.d: A strategic ownership system where players or teams capture, contest, defend, and exploit map regions for resources, scoring, visibility, movement, or production.
e: Two teams enter the region on the same tick and capture progress must stop or reverse.
The owning team disconnects or changes alliance while income is being awarded.
A region is captured while hidden under fog of war and needs partial disclosure.
b: Capture progress continues after the capture source dies or leaves the region.
Income is granted to the old owner for one extra tick after transfer.
UI overlays update before authority accepts the ownership transaction.
t: Capture pace controls whether territory rewards aggression, defense, or coordinated pushes.
High income regions should be exposed enough to create counterplay.
a: Show ownership and contested state through shape, text, pattern, and audio cues in addition to color.
Provide map overlays that can be paused or inspected without losing important capture information.

strategy.unit_counter_system.d: A strategic combat relationship model where unit types, weapons, armor, abilities, or formations gain advantages and disadvantages against specific opponent categories.
p: counter_type_id: cavalry, armored, flying, infantry, shielded
target_entity_id: enemy unit, structure, squad, monster
e: A unit has multiple counter types and receives conflicting modifiers.
A tech unlock changes a matchup while projectiles or attacks are already in flight.
A shapeshifted, upgraded, or garrisoned unit should expose different counter categories.
b: Damage modifiers apply twice because both weapon and target code read the same table.
Tooltip matchup text uses old data after balance patches.
Unit categories are localized strings and do not match damage_modifier_table_id keys.
t: Hard counters create clear decisions but can punish players who lack scouting or production flexibility.
Soft counters preserve unit identity while leaving room for upgrades, terrain, and micro decisions.
a: Show matchup explanations in text and icon form, not only through color-coded arrows.
Provide compact and expanded tooltip modes for high information density.

survival.base_building.d: Players place, upgrade, persist, and defend structures that provide storage, shelter, crafting, or territory control.
p: ownership_permission_id: owner, clan, public, raid_allowed, decay_unclaimed
e: Destroying a foundation removes support for child structures that contain inventories, queues, or sleeping players.
A player places a structure while terrain, navmesh, or another player-built piece changes underneath it.
A shelter volume is partially enclosed and systems disagree whether rain, cold, enemies, or spawns are blocked.
b: Placement preview accepts a location but server validation rejects it due to different collision or slope checks.
Structures persist visually but ownership, inventory links, or crafting station queues are lost after load.
Navmesh and AI spawn blockers are not rebuilt after base edits, letting enemies spawn inside sealed rooms.
t: Base safety should reward planning without removing all survival pressure from weather, raids, or resource needs.
Upkeep and decay can control server clutter, but opaque decay feels punishing when players return after a break.
a: Provide clear placement previews with text reasons for blocked placement, support failure, or permission denial.
Support keyboard and controller placement nudging, rotation steps, and snap toggles for precise building.

survival.day_night_cycle.d: A survival world-clock driver changes pressure through visibility, enemy activity, temperature, sleep rules, safe zones, and scheduled resource consequences.
p: survival_phase_id: dawn, day, dusk, night, blood_moon
e: A player enters a dungeon, cave, or base where world lighting changes should not fully apply.
Multiplayer players disagree on sleeping, skipping, or accelerating the night phase.
Night starts while crafting queues, raids, temperature shifts, or AI spawn groups are already pending.
b: Lighting phase changes but AI and temperature still use the previous survival_phase_id.
Sleep skip advances the world clock but does not advance hunger, thirst, crafting queues, or enemy despawn rules consistently.
Night warnings repeat after load because the previous warning timestamp was not persisted.
t: Night should be threatening enough to change behavior, but not so punishing that players simply wait through it.
If sleeping skips danger, require preparation or tradeoffs such as bed safety, hunger, or multiplayer agreement.
a: Communicate phase and incoming danger through text, icons, audio, and lighting, not darkness alone.
Offer visibility, contrast, or reduced-night-danger settings for players who struggle with dark scenes.

survival.durability.d: Items track condition and lose durability through use, damage, or environment until they require repair or break.
e: An item breaks during the same action that gathers resources, deals damage, or blocks an attack.
Repair materials are consumed but the item instance is moved, traded, or destroyed during the transaction.
Stacked items share one icon but contain different durability_item_id values and condition states.
b: Durability is stored on the item definition, so all copies of the tool lose condition together.
Broken items still pass action validation because only UI checks condition thresholds.
Repair preview and repair transaction use different material costs or restored condition rules.
t: Fast gear wear can add survival tension, but it becomes frustrating if repair materials are scarce or unclear.
Durability works best when players can choose between cheap disposable tools and costly reliable equipment.
a: Show durability with numbers or labels in addition to bars or color.
Provide repair prompts or warning reminders before players enter long routes with nearly broken key gear.

survival.health.d: A core vitality and failure state that resolves damage, healing, downed/death transitions, and recovery from combat, hazards, disease, starvation, dehydration, and exposure.
p: damage_channel_id: bleed, starvation, cold, melee, poison, fall
recovery_source_id: bandage, medkit, cooked_meal, sleep, regen_aura
e: Starvation, dehydration, cold, poison, and combat damage resolve on the same tick and must produce one ordered health transaction.
A healing item is used while the player is entering a downed, revive, or death transition.
Temporary max-health reduction changes current health, death threshold, and UI warnings after save/load.
b: Damage over time stacks every frame because survival ticks are not rate-limited by damage_channel_id or damage_transaction_id.
Healing consumes items but fails when max health modifiers update during the same transaction.
Death logic fires twice and creates duplicate drops, ragdolls, revive prompts, or respawn checkpoints.
t: Health should give players enough buffer to diagnose survival problems before dying.
Passive regeneration can reduce frustration but may weaken hunger, thirst, and medicine loops.
a: Show damage source text or icons when health is lost from survival systems, not only combat.
Offer reduced screen blood, pulse effects, or low-health audio intensity while preserving readable danger cues.

survival.hunger.d: A long-term metabolic survival stat that decays through a survival clock, recovers through food transactions, and applies nutrition thresholds or starvation penalties.
e: A player consumes food while taking starvation damage in the same simulation tick.
Offline decay, sleeping, or fast travel advances hunger without giving the player a chance to respond.
Food restores hunger but also applies poison, spoilage, warmth, hydration, or temporary well-fed effects.
b: Hunger decay runs during paused menus or loading screens because it reads a wall clock instead of survival clock state.
Food is removed from inventory but recovery is not applied when a capacity or status-effect transaction fails.
UI warning bands display stale hunger after server correction or save-load restoration.
t: Fast decay can make survival tense, but it quickly becomes busywork if food sources are common and decisions are shallow.
Low hunger penalties are usually easier to tune than instant death because they give players recovery space.
a: Provide clear warning bands, optional numeric display, and non-color cues before hunger becomes dangerous.
Offer relaxed decay settings or assist modes for players who prefer exploration over resource upkeep.

survival.inventory_limit.d: Inventory space, weight, slots, or containers limit how much the player can carry during survival play.
e: Crafting consumes several ingredients and produces an output that no longer fits the container.
A player picks up a stackable item while another transaction splits or moves the same stack.
Weight modifiers from equipment, hunger, injuries, or companions update while inventory UI is open.
b: Capacity validation runs after item pickup, creating negative slots or overweight states that cannot be resolved.
Stack splitting loses item_instance_id metadata such as durability, quality, or ownership.
Server and client sort inventory differently, causing drag transactions to move the wrong slot.
t: Strict limits make every expedition strategic, but excessive shuffling can become the dominant play activity.
Storage upgrades should reduce friction without eliminating the need to choose route goals.
a: Provide sortable lists, readable capacity text, and controller-friendly slot navigation.
Use warnings before rejecting or dropping items so players understand capacity failures.

survival.oxygen.d: A breath and volume state depletes in unsafe spaces such as underwater, vacuum, smoke, or toxic air, then recovers through breathable volumes or refill sources.
p: oxygen_depletion_per_second: 0.5-10 seconds of air per second
e: The player crosses the waterline repeatedly and the oxygen UI flickers between drain and refill states.
A vehicle, base, or cave counts as breathable while the surrounding volume remains hazardous.
Surfacing, climbing out, or entering an air pocket restores breath while drowning damage is already queued.
b: Oxygen drains while the player is paused or in loading screens because the unsafe volume state remains active.
Refill logic runs every frame and repeatedly plays warning-clear audio or particles.
Drowning damage begins before the zero-oxygen warning animation has completed.
t: Short oxygen windows create strong tension but need nearby readable recovery options.
Equipment upgrades can extend exploration range without removing the need to plan routes.
a: Use numeric countdown, icon state, audio, and optional haptics for oxygen warnings.
Avoid relying only on muffled audio or vignette effects, and offer reduced panic effects for sensitive players.

survival.stamina.d: A regenerating exertion resource gates accepted actions, exhaustion lockout, and recovery timing for movement, attacks, blocks, climbs, or survival tasks.
e: A buffered dodge, attack, or jump becomes valid on the same frame stamina recovers above the action threshold.
Sprinting spends stamina while climbing, swimming, blocking, or carrying weight also applies modifiers.
A partial-threshold action such as light attack, short climb, or slow swim remains valid while full-cost actions are exhausted.
b: Regeneration starts immediately after a spend because stamina_regen_delay_ms is checked against render frames.
Failed actions still spend stamina when validation order is input, cost, then collision or state rejection.
Exhaustion state never clears after save/load because last spend tick or regen lockout was not persisted.
t: Low stamina capacity makes route planning tense, but too much restriction can make basic traversal feel punitive.
Separate combat and traversal costs if one loop is starving the other of player agency.
a: Provide optional stamina assist, wider input buffering, or slower depletion for players who cannot sustain rapid inputs.
Use clear UI and audio states for exhaustion without relying only on heavy camera sway or breathing effects.

survival.temperature.d: An environmental exposure state samples zones, weather, wetness, shelter, clothing, and heat or cold sources before applying survival penalties.
p: exposure_threshold_id: comfortable, chilly, freezing, overheating, heatstroke
e: The player crosses multiple temperature zones while inside a vehicle, cave, or player-built shelter.
Wetness from swimming or rain persists through fast travel, sleeping, or save/load restoration.
A heat source warms the player but does not protect food, water, companions, or nearby crafting stations.
b: Exposure damage starts before UI warning thresholds appear because warning and penalty tables use different ids.
Shelter detection checks only roof collision and ignores open walls, wind direction, or structure ownership.
Insulation modifiers stack permanently when equipment is swapped quickly.
t: Exposure should ramp through warning, penalty, and danger bands rather than jumping directly to health loss.
Harsh zones work best when players have at least one clear preparation path: clothing, shelter, food, heat, or route timing.
a: Do not rely only on screen tint or particle effects; show exposure reason, severity, and recovery source in readable UI.
Offer reduced exposure severity or longer warning buffers for players who need more planning time.

survival.thirst.d: A hydration survival stat that usually decays faster than hunger, reacts to heat or exertion, and recovers through validated water sources, drinks, or containers.
e: A player drinks from a source while inventory capacity changes the container or empty bottle state.
Rain, swimming, or shelter changes hydration context but should not automatically refill the stat.
Hot temperature zones, fever, or sprinting multiply thirst decay while pause, sleep, or fast-travel policy is active.
b: Drinking consumes a container but fails to apply hydration because source validation happens after item mutation.
Contamination effects apply even when the purification recipe or filter item was used successfully.
Thirst warnings spam every frame near the same threshold instead of using threshold crossing events.
t: Thirst usually feels more urgent than hunger; tune warnings early enough for players to seek water before penalties start.
Purification and containers add meaningful planning only when safe and unsafe sources are visually distinct.
a: Use text labels, icons, and optional audio warnings so hydration state is not conveyed only by screen effects.
Allow reduced dehydration penalties or slower decay for players who find constant upkeep stressful.

time.cooldown_time.d: A reusable action becomes unavailable after activation, then returns after a tracked recharge interval.
p: started_at_server_ms: server timestamp or monotonic tick
e: An activation request arrives twice from buffered input, rollback resimulation, or a delayed network packet.
The player saves, loads, dies, or changes equipment while one or more charges are partially recovered.
A pause menu uses unscaled_time while the recharge scheduler uses gameplay_clock_id, causing UI and authority state to disagree.
b: The UI displays zero remaining milliseconds before the authority state accepts a new activation.
Recharge progress resets when the owning entity is pooled, respawned, or migrated to a different network owner.
Client prediction grants an action locally, then the server rejects it because started_at_server_ms was stale.
t: Short intervals make the action part of the base rhythm; long intervals turn it into a deliberate commitment.
Shared lockouts are useful for preventing optimal rotations, but they can make loadouts feel samey if every strong tool blocks every other tool.
a: Pair radial fills with numeric or icon state changes so readiness is not communicated only by color or motion.
Allow input buffering near the final recharge window for players who cannot repeatedly tap at exact readiness frames.

time.day_night_schedule.d: A world schedule advances through named phases that can drive lighting, spawns, NPC routines, and gameplay gates.
e: A save file loads during a transition blend while lighting has advanced but NPC schedules have not.
Fast travel or sleeping skips over a phase that contains a quest trigger, spawn rule, or survival hazard.
Multiplayer clients join with clock drift and briefly see different enemy or lighting states.
b: Lighting, audio, and weather subscribe to different phase names and become desynchronized after acceleration.
NPC schedules run multiple missed phase events at once after load and teleport actors into invalid spaces.
Server and client clocks round the phase fraction differently, causing doors, vendors, or hazards to disagree.
t: Long cycles support exploration and planning; short cycles create constant pressure but can make travel feel rushed.
Night hazards should be matched with readable preparation options such as shelter, light, or alternate routes.
a: Do not communicate phase changes only through color temperature; include icons, labels, audio, or environmental cues.
Offer gentler night contrast or visibility settings when the schedule materially affects navigation.

time.rhythm_timing.d: Player input is evaluated against a beat grid or scheduled cue, producing graded results based on offset.
e: Audio playback drifts from the simulation clock after device sleep, tab throttling, pause, or buffer underrun.
Input buffering captures a press before a scene transition and replays it against the next chart section.
Frame drops delay visual hit markers while audio and judgment state already advanced.
b: Judgment uses frame delta instead of the audio clock, making the same input grade differently across hardware.
Calibration offset is applied twice to held notes or not applied to release events.
The hit marker displays the predicted grade but combo state uses the corrected authority result.
t: Wider windows increase approachability, but too much width can erase the distinction between intentional rhythm and random tapping.
Separate scoring strictness from progression requirements so players can finish content without needing expert timing.
a: Provide audio, visual, and optional haptic beat cues, and allow players to calibrate display and input latency.
Offer reduced precision modes or wider judgment tables without changing the song or encounter structure.

time.slow_motion.d: Selected gameplay systems run at a reduced simulation scale while input, UI, or audio may remain responsive.
e: Projectiles, hitboxes, particles, and animation notifies run on different clocks during the slowed window.
The effect begins while a cooldown, rhythm judgment, or timed challenge is using another clock source.
A multiplayer client predicts slow motion locally even though the server rejects the trigger.
b: UI prompts and input buffering become sluggish because they were accidentally attached to the scaled gameplay clock.
Audio pitch drops for dialogue or accessibility cues that should remain intelligible.
Animation events fire at scaled playback while weapon traces still use unscaled frame deltas.
t: Lower simulation scale gives dramatic readability but can trivialize aiming, dodging, and puzzle execution.
Limit availability through resource cost, trigger rarity, or encounter-specific rules if slow motion solves too many threats.
a: Allow players to reduce or disable motion distortion, heavy screen effects, and audio pitch shifts during slow motion.
Consider optional assist settings that provide slower reaction windows without tying them to flashy camera effects.

time.time_freeze.d: A freeze suspends selected actors, projectiles, hazards, or simulation channels while exempt systems continue running.
p: affected_channel_mask: animation, ai, projectiles, rigidbodies, particles
e: A frozen rigidbody is moved by the player, then released with stale velocity or overlapping collision shapes.
A freeze starts while an AI, animation montage, or ability transaction is halfway through a state transition.
Objective timers, cooldowns, and rhythm charts disagree about whether the freeze should pause them.
b: Frozen actors still receive damage ticks, status effects, or scripted callbacks from unpaused systems.
Release restores velocity but not angular velocity, sleeping state, animation phase, or particle emission state.
Hit detection runs against the visually frozen pose while the authority simulation has already resumed.
t: A full global freeze is usually stronger than a slow-motion effect because it removes enemy reaction entirely.
Bosses and objectives may need resistance or shortened windows, but exemptions should be visible and consistent.
a: Avoid intense flashing, sudden audio dropouts, or heavy color inversion as the only freeze indication.
If the freeze creates planning space, provide enough UI clarity for players using slower input methods.

time.time_rewind.d: Previously recorded state snapshots are replayed backward or restored to an earlier point under player or system control.
p: recorded_state_channel: player_transform, velocity, health, object_state, projectile_state
e: A rewind tries to restore an object that has been destroyed, pooled, unloaded, or replaced by a streamed chunk.
Random events, loot drops, or network messages occurred during the rewound interval and must not be duplicated.
The restored collision pose intersects moving platforms, doors, enemies, or newly spawned objects.
b: Only transform state is recorded, so velocity, animation phase, health, cooldowns, and AI blackboard state resume incorrectly.
Snapshot buffers grow without bounds when multiple actors enter the recorded_state_channel set.
Restored physics bodies wake with stale contact pairs and launch the player after the first solver step.
t: Long buffers encourage experimentation but can remove tension unless objectives or resources define what remains irreversible.
Full-world rewind is expensive and powerful; single-channel rewind is easier to balance but must be communicated clearly.
a: Rewind can be a strong accessibility aid when it reduces repetitive failure loops; expose clear availability and remaining history.
Provide reduced motion and reduced audio-scrub options for players sensitive to reversed camera or sound effects.

time.timed_challenge.d: A challenge starts from a defined trigger and requires success before a visible deadline expires.
e: The player pauses, opens a dialogue, or triggers a cutscene while the challenge is already active.
A success event and expiry event occur in the same simulation tick or arrive in different orders over the network.
Checkpoint reload restores player position but not spawned enemies, doors, or collected objective items.
b: Start triggers fire multiple times and reset the countdown after the player has already begun the route.
Failure logic runs on the client and server, duplicating penalties, rewards, or reset effects.
The timer keeps advancing during loading screens because it reads a wall clock instead of the gameplay clock.
t: The best limit usually gives skilled players room for one small mistake while still rewarding route knowledge.
If the challenge is required for progression, provide retry speed and checkpoint placement that respects repeated attempts.
a: Expose countdown information through text, icon state, and optional audio cues rather than relying only on color or flashing.
Offer relaxed limits or assist modes for players who need more planning or input execution time.

traversal.gliding.d: A controlled aerial traversal state that reduces fall velocity and uses lift, drag, stamina, wind, or pitch input to extend airborne travel.
e: Glide activation near a ceiling or wall needs a blocked-start result instead of clipping the character upward.
Landing on moving platforms, slopes, or water needs a clear transition into grounded, sliding, or swimming states.
Wind zones should not stack into infinite lift unless the level is authored for it.
b: Fall velocity cap applies after collision and lets the player sink through thin floors.
Stamina drains while glide input is held even after landing.
Camera pitch follows the glider too aggressively and creates motion discomfort.
t: Glide availability changes how every high point functions as a route start.
Resource drain and fall velocity cap determine whether gliding is exploration, escape, or precision traversal.
a: Provide camera comfort options for pitch lock, reduced sway, and toned-down field-of-view shifts.
Offer aim or steering assists for long glides that require sustained fine analog control.

traversal.grappling_hook.d: A traversal tool that validates a distant anchor, attaches the player to it, then pulls, reels, swings, or redirects momentum through explicit detach rules.
e: Moving anchors must define whether the player inherits anchor velocity and what happens when the anchor is destroyed.
Rope paths around corners need wrapping, collision shortening, or detachment rules.
A grapple that ends inside geometry needs a safe landing probe or rollback point.
b: Anchor validation uses camera ray hits but movement pulls toward a different physics point.
Rope length goes negative near the anchor and launches the player.
Canceling during attach leaves gravity, input lock, or collision masks in grapple state.
t: Long anchor distance and strong snap assist make grapple a navigation default; limited anchors make it a route puzzle.
Reel velocity, detach freedom, and fall recovery determine whether grapple is traversal, combat escape, or both.
a: Use strong anchor highlighting and optional snap assist so players can identify valid targets quickly.
Provide input buffering for release and avoid requiring tiny moving-target aim unless alternate controls exist.

traversal.jetpack.d: A powered traversal state that spends fuel or heat capacity to apply controllable lift and steering while airborne.
p: thrust_vector_units: upward plus optional forward component
e: Fuel can expire over a lethal pit, requiring a clear fall, glide, or ledge recovery path.
Ceiling collision while thrusting must stop lift without trapping the player in powered state.
Water volumes, low-gravity zones, and wind zones need explicit interaction rules with thrust_vector_units.
b: Thrust is applied in render update and becomes stronger at high frame rates.
Fuel drains after landing because airborne_state_machine does not clear jetpack input ownership.
Heat lockout clears on client but not server, causing repeated correction snaps.
t: Fuel capacity controls whether jetpack is a correction tool, route tool, or full movement mode.
Hover makes aiming and platforming easier but can trivialize hazards unless fuel drain rises sharply.
a: Offer reduced camera shake, field-of-view, and vertical bob while powered movement is active.
Allow hold or toggle thrust settings and readable fuel warnings that do not rely only on color.

traversal.ladder_climb.d: A constrained vertical traversal state that attaches the character to a ladder, maps input to rung movement, and handles safe entry and exit points.
e: The top exit can be blocked after the player starts climbing, requiring a hold, drop, or retry state.
Two players or AI agents can attach to the same ladder segment in multiplayer or crowd scenes.
Jumping off a ladder needs a clear impulse vector and restored collision layers.
b: The character remains in no-gravity mode after detaching from ladder_id.
Input axis mapping flips when camera direction crosses behind the ladder.
Exit placement ignores capsule clearance and clips the player into the floor above.
t: Fast ladders reduce frustration but make vertical exposure and combat risk less meaningful.
Auto-attach is useful in tight spaces but can steal control near ledges or interactables.
a: Allow simple up/down input and avoid requiring held diagonal inputs to stay attached.
Use distinct visual and audio cues for valid exit points, not only camera angle or controller vibration.

traversal.mantling.d: A ledge recovery action that detects a valid edge, snaps the character to it, and moves them onto the upper surface through scripted or root-motion alignment.
e: The ledge can be valid from the camera ray but blocked by collision at the landing point.
Moving platforms need ledge_snap_position relative to the platform, not only world coordinates.
A player may request mantle while carrying objects, aiming, knocked back, or under stamina exhaustion.
b: Mantle starts from a decorative edge with no safe landing surface.
Root motion pushes the character through collision because the sweep is disabled during the montage.
Camera clips into the ledge when vertical correction is large.
t: Wide snap distance makes traversal forgiving but can feel magnetic around unintended ledges.
Auto-mantle improves flow in action games but can steal player control near hazards or stealth cover.
a: Expose optional auto-mantle or extended input buffering for players who struggle with precise ledge timing.
Avoid sudden camera lifts during mantle, or provide reduced camera motion settings.

traversal.parkour_vault.d: A committed traversal action that detects a low obstacle, validates approach and clearance, then moves the character over it through scripted or root-motion movement.
e: The obstacle is valid but the landing side becomes blocked by another actor or moving object.
Vault activation near interact prompts, cover, or ledges needs a priority rule so intent is not misread.
Root motion vaults must handle moving platforms or doors that shift under the animation.
b: Vault casts detect decorative trim and launch the player over unintended geometry.
The animation moves through collision because collision sweeps are disabled during the montage.
Camera transition collides with walls and hides the landing point.
t: Generous auto-vault improves flow but can remove tactical cover if every low wall becomes pass-through.
Long vault animations are cinematic but risky in combat unless protected or cancelable.
a: Provide manual-vault or auto-vault options depending on how often obstacles appear.
Keep camera changes subtle and include clear affordance markings for vaultable obstacles.

traversal.rope_swing.d: A traversal state where the player is attached to a rope or pivot and moves along an arc under gravity and input.
e: Rope collision can wrap around corners, clip through geometry, or force detachment; choose one behavior.
Release during pause, hit stop, or slow motion should use one authoritative velocity sample.
The player hitting a ceiling or wall mid-swing needs clear bounce, slide, or detach behavior.
b: Swing input adds world-horizontal force instead of tangential force and breaks the arc.
Rope length drifts over time because constraints are corrected after integration without projection.
Release velocity is sampled after collision correction and launches in the wrong direction.
t: Higher damping makes swings forgiving but less expressive; low damping rewards timing and route planning.
Large release impulse increases spectacle but can invalidate nearby platform spacing.
a: Provide clear release direction cues and consider wider landing areas when swing timing is mandatory.
Avoid camera swings that track the arc too aggressively; motion-sensitive players need stable horizon options.

traversal.teleport_blink.d: A short-range teleport that instantly relocates the player to a validated destination.
e: Destination validation must reject walls, thin ceilings, moving hazards, occupied spaces, and out-of-bounds voids.
Blinking across navmesh gaps should decide whether enemies can follow or retain targeting.
Momentum, projectiles, grapples, and status effects need rules for whether they persist through blink.
b: The destination marker is valid in the preview but invalid when the player confirms due to stale collision data.
Blink preserves downward velocity and instantly kills the player after arrival.
Arrival effects spawn at the origin because teleport state clears before presentation events read it.
t: Long-range blink bypasses level geometry and enemy zoning; cooldown and destination validation become major balance levers.
If blink grants invulnerability or attack canceling, tune it as both traversal and defense.
a: Show a clear valid/invalid destination indicator using more than color, and allow confirm-to-blink for precision modes.
Avoid disorienting camera snaps; preserve facing or offer a predictable recenter option after teleport.

traversal.vehicle_mount.d: An interaction that transfers a character into a vehicle seat, assigns driver or passenger authority, and validates safe exit when leaving.
e: Two players request the same seat in the same server tick and need deterministic tie-breaking.
The vehicle moves during the entry animation and changes the mount transform.
Exit positions can be blocked by walls, hazards, water, or enemy bodies.
b: Client grants driver control before the server approves seat_id ownership.
Entry animation completes but collision handoff leaves the character capsule active inside the vehicle.
Exit validation places the player under the vehicle or inside a nearby wall.
t: Long entry windows create vulnerability; instant entry improves usability but can enable escape exploits.
Seat ownership rules matter in co-op and PvP because players can grief by stealing driver seats.
a: Use clear seat prompts with driver/passenger labels and remappable interaction input.
Avoid rapid camera snaps on mount or dismount; provide comfort settings for vehicle camera transitions.

traversal.wall_run.d: A traversal state where the player temporarily runs along a valid wall while gravity and steering are modified.
e: Curved or uneven walls can rapidly change normals and should use smoothing or segmented eligibility.
Inside corners need explicit behavior: transfer, stop, jump, or detach.
Damage, stun, landing, water entry, and cutscenes must clear reduced gravity and camera roll.
b: The player sticks to decorative walls because surface tags are not checked.
Gravity suppression remains active after the state exits.
Exit jump uses camera forward instead of wall normal and launches unpredictably.
t: Long wall runs can replace intended routes unless surface tags, stamina, or distance caps constrain them.
Entry velocity requirements make wall run a momentum skill rather than a universal climb.
a: Provide reduced camera roll and FOV options, plus consistent visual language for runnable walls.
Avoid requiring exact approach angles without forgiving attach windows or route alternatives.

traversal.zipline.d: A traversal route where the player attaches to a cable or rail and moves along a predefined line between endpoints.
e: Endpoint landing space can become blocked by enemies, moving platforms, or other players.
Detaching mid-route should preserve route velocity in a predictable direction.
Multiple players on the same zipline need spacing, collision, or overlap rules.
b: The player remains parented to the zipline after detach and cannot move normally.
Cable progress overshoots the endpoint and reverses or jitters.
Camera faces the route direction but input still uses world movement axes.
t: Fast ziplines compress travel time but can bypass encounter space unless endpoints are controlled.
Manual detach adds expression but can create unintended shortcuts if landing areas are not tested.
a: Use clear attach prompts and endpoint visibility so players know where the ride leads before committing.
Avoid strong camera banking on ziplines unless reduced-motion settings can disable it.

ui_ux.accessibility_remap_controls.d: A control settings interface that lets players rebind input actions across keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touch, or accessibility devices with conflict handling and persistence.
p: input_action_id: jump, interact, sprint, fire, inventory
e: A player unbinds confirm, cancel, pause, or menu navigation and needs a recovery path.
Two local players remap controls on one device and must not overwrite each other.
A platform reserves a button or key that the game exposes in its default binding list.
b: Prompt glyphs keep showing default bindings after the player remaps input.
Conflict resolution updates the visible row but not the actual input map consumed by gameplay.
Reset defaults applies to keyboard but leaves gamepad or touch bindings stale.
t: Remapping should generally be allowed in ranked modes because it changes access, not action strength.
Some competitive games may restrict macros or multi-action bindings, but should explain that boundary clearly.
a: Support keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touch, and adaptive controller profiles where the platform allows it.
Keep remap UI navigable without relying on the binding being changed; always provide reset and cancel paths.

ui_ux.checkpoint_notification.d: A save-state feedback notification that projects authoritative checkpoint, autosave, or manual save transaction status through queued UI, icon, text, audio, and failure-state handling.
p: checkpoint_saved_at_ms: unix epoch or session milliseconds
e: The save starts but fails after the notification has already shown success.
Repeated checkpoint triggers in one room should not spam the notification queue.
Cloud sync, cross-save, or network profiles can have local commit success and remote sync failure.
b: Notification fires when checkpoint trigger is entered, not when the save transaction commits.
Save failed messages are hidden behind higher-priority combat or quest notifications.
Checkpoint icon persists forever because duplicate suppression cancels the hide event.
t: Checkpoint feedback should be noticeable enough to reassure players but not so large that it interrupts repeated retries.
Save failure deserves stronger priority than save success because it changes player risk.
a: Use icon, text, and optional audio together; do not rely only on a tiny animated save symbol.
Respect reduced-motion settings for pulsing save icons and support readable text scaling.

ui_ux.cooldown_indicator.d: A state-bound UI element that projects authoritative action availability, remaining cooldown, charge count, and disabled state for an ability, item, weapon, or input action.
e: Cooldown resets, haste effects, pause, slow motion, and server correction can change the remaining time mid-animation.
Shared cooldown groups need one visible source of truth across multiple abilities and loadout slots.
Charge-based abilities should show partial readiness without implying all charges are restored.
b: UI countdown uses local time while gameplay cooldown uses simulation time and drifts during pause.
Cooldown fill reaches zero visually before the server accepts the action.
Ready flash plays after the ability was removed, swapped, or disabled by silence.
t: Exact timers make optimization easier; vague fills preserve uncertainty and reduce UI pressure.
High-stakes defensive cooldowns need stronger feedback than low-impact convenience actions.
a: Use shape, icon state, numeric text, and optional audio rather than color alone.
Allow scaling or simplified cooldown displays when many abilities are visible at once.

ui_ux.damage_numbers.d: Floating, anchored, or logged combat values projected from committed damage events to explain amount, type, mitigation, healing, shields, critical hits, or resisted effects.
e: Damage over time and area attacks can create dozens of numbers per second unless merged or rate-limited.
Large enemies need anchor points so numbers do not appear inside geometry or offscreen.
Negative, immune, absorbed, overheal, and blocked results need different display rules.
b: Numbers spawn from raw collision events and appear even when damage was blocked.
World-space labels sort behind walls or enemy meshes.
Stacked values merge across different targets because the grouping key is incomplete.
t: Verbose numbers encourage optimization and build comparison; minimal numbers preserve immersion and reduce clutter.
Showing resisted or absorbed values helps players understand enemy defenses without external spreadsheets.
a: Provide size, opacity, motion, and disable options for floating numbers.
Use text labels or icons for damage categories instead of color alone.

ui_ux.dialogue_choice.d: A UI interaction where the player selects a response or decision during dialogue.
e: Timed choices during pause, subtitle review, or accessibility menus need fair timer behavior.
Locked choices should not leak spoilers unless the design intentionally shows requirements.
Voiceover, subtitle text, and abbreviated choice labels can imply different meanings if not reviewed together.
b: Controller focus defaults to a destructive or costly choice.
Choice requirements are checked for display but not again when selected.
Localized text overflows and hides cost or reputation requirements.
t: Showing exact consequences supports planning; hiding them supports role-play and uncertainty.
Skill or reputation choices should feel like payoff for prior investment, not mandatory optimal routes.
a: Support subtitle sizing, dialogue history, timer disable options, and clear focus indicators.
Avoid presenting tone icons without text labels for players who cannot infer icon meaning.

ui_ux.hit_marker.d: A short visual or audio confirmation projected from an authoritative hit or damage result, keyed by attacker, target, projectile, and combat outcome.
e: Damage over time should not spam hit markers every tick unless the design intentionally wants that feedback.
Stealth, smoke, darkness, or hidden targets may need suppressed markers to avoid revealing information.
Shotguns and area effects need merge rules so audio and markers do not stack excessively.
b: Marker plays on blocked, immune, or friendly hits because any overlap counts.
Critical marker appears for overkill damage rather than weak-point metadata.
Marker sound is mixed too loudly when many pellets hit at once.
t: Strong hit markers improve readability but can reveal targets through smoke, darkness, or cover.
Different marker types should communicate important combat state, not cosmetic complexity.
a: Provide visual and audio confirmation options independently, with color-safe marker shapes.
Allow hit marker size, opacity, and sound volume to be adjusted separately from damage numbers.

ui_ux.interaction_prompt.d: A target-bound affordance cue that projects the current interactable_id, action_id, input binding, enabled state, and hold/tap requirement for the player who owns focus.
p: interaction_action_id: open, talk, pickup, mount, repair
e: Overlapping interactables need stable candidate selection, focus ownership, and optional cycling.
A target can become invalid, locked, destroyed, or authority-rejected after button press but before hold completion.
Prompts must update when controls are remapped, input devices change, or local co-op players swap focus.
b: Prompt displays one binding while the input system expects another.
Focus flickers between objects at the edge of activation distance.
The prompt says open but the interaction performs pick up because candidate data is stale.
